info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:

before.title: Before

date_type.description:

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1

    StandardAge:

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed

        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Has anyone measured creep, stress-rupture or long-exposure (1000 h or more) thermal stability at 250 C or above for a laser powder bed fusion aluminum alloy that contains no scandium, such as Al-Ce, Al-Fe-Zr, Al-Ni-Zr, Al-Mn-Zr or Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys?

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
<jats:p>As a new alloy manufacturing method that can break through the limitations of molds to manufacture fine parts, laser powder bed fusion has recently become a common process for producing aluminum alloys. In the fields of aerospace or automotive, aluminum alloys with both good printability and good mechanical performance in high-temperature conditions are greatly demanded, and the Al-Ce alloy is one of the alloys with significant potential. Therefore, systematic research on the additive manufacturing of Al-Ce alloys is still being explored. Herein, we review the recent progress and current status of laser powder bed fusion-produced Al-Ce alloys, giving our opinions on the development of this alloy system. Element composition, alloy powders, laser powder bed fusion parameters, microstructures, and mechanical properties at room temperature and high temperatures are summarized. The choice of alloying strategies is crucial for a specific mechanical improvement of the Al-Ce alloys. Finally, the details of the Al-Ce alloys manufactured via laser powder bed fusion are presented.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Aluminum alloys containing small amounts of cerium have been investigated to improve the grain refining, casting characteristics, and mechanical properties of aluminum alloys. These additions were usually made at levels of 1% or less but did not produce appreciable improvements. Recent work has shown that additions between 4% and the approximate eutectic composition of 10% improve the high-temperature performance of aluminum alloys. Corrosion performance of aluminum alloys can also be improved through the addition of Ce. Traditional aluminum alloying elements such as magnesium and silicon can be used to control casting characteristics and thermal and physical properties. Cerium oxide is the predominate oxide in rare earth mining. Much of it is discarded after separation from the heavy rare earth oxides containing Nd and Dy. The beneficial use of Ce should reduce the cost of the more desirable rare earths. Results of using Ce as an addition to aluminum in mul-tiple manufacturing methods such as additive manufacturing, extrusion, and casting are explored. The results show significant strengthening and improved mechanical property retention at higher temperatures than in other aluminum alloys and, in some compositions, show complete recovery of mechanical properties at room temperature when exposed to elevated temperatures as high as 500°C for 1000 hours.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Driven by the rapid advancement of key engineering domains such as aerospace, transportation, and marine systems, there is an urgent need for aluminum alloys exhibiting superior mechanical properties. Heterostructures, defined by inhomogeneous distributions of microstructural domains with distinct property gradients, have become a leading strategy to achieve a synergy between outstanding strength and satisfactory ductility. Additive manufacturing technologies, particularly laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), provide unparalleled design flexibility for creating heterogeneous microstructures. This review systematically classifies the various heterostructures in additively manufactured aluminum alloys, investigates the mechanisms enabling precise control of microstructural heterogeneity, and underscores the exceptional mechanical performance of L-PBF-processed alloys with such structures. Moreover, the challenges and opportunities associated with advancing heterostructured aluminum alloys via L-PBF are critically analyzed, highlighting the necessity for robust theoretical frameworks and scalable manufacturing approaches.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Inconel 718 (IN718) is a polycrystalline nickel-based superalloy and one of the most widely used materials in the aerospace industry owing to its excellent mechanical performances at high temperatures, including creep resistance. Interest in additively manufactured components in aerospace is greatly increasing due to their ability to reduce material consumption, to manufacture complex parts, and to produce out-of-equilibrium microstructures, which can be beneficial for mechanical behavior. IN718’s properties are, however, very sensitive to microstructural features, which strongly depend on the manufacturing process and subsequent heat treatments. Additive manufacturing and, more specifically, Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) induces very high thermal gradients and anisotropic features due to its inherently directional nature, which largely defines the microstructure of the alloy. Hence, defining appropriate manufacturing parameters and heat treatments is critical to obtain appropriate mechanical behavior. This review aims to present the main microstructural features of IN718 produced by LPBF, the creep mechanisms taking place, the optimal microstructure for creep strength, and the most efficient heat treatments to yield such an optimized microstructure.

Abstract:
The introduction of Sc/Zr inoculates to aluminium (Al) alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) provides numerous benefits, including laser processability improvement, solidification microstructure control and mechanical property enhancement. Though great efforts have been put into tailoring the microstructure and room temperature mechanical properties via process parameter optimisations, the potential roles of Sc/Zr inoculate modified Al alloys for high-temperature applications were still underexplored. In this study, the microstructural stability and the elevated temperature tensile behaviours of LPBF-processed Al-Mn-Sc alloy were systematically evaluated. The alloy demonstrated high microstructural stability after both heat treatment and high-temperature tensile testing for up to 573 K. The applied tensile testing temperature and strain rate played significant influences on the elevated temperature tensile properties and deformation behaviours. Unusual intermediate temperature embrittlement (also known as ductility dip) and yield drop behaviours were observed under certain testing temperature and strain rate regimes, and the underlying deformation mechanisms were elucidated in detail. The present study is expected to shed light on future high-performance, high-temperature Al alloy development for the LPBF process.

Abstract:
Processing 7075 alloy by laser powder bed fusion is complex due to hot cracking. Zr addition is one of the solutions to reduce this susceptibility to cracking and permit the elaboration of crack-free parts. This study explored the microstructural and hardness evolutions of an Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr alloy with respect to different heat treatment routes. In particular, natural and artificial agings are considered from as-built and solution heat-treated tempers. Microstructural characterization was principally carried out by optical, scanning, and transmission electron microscopy. In the as-built state, the melt pools exhibited a bimodal grain structure consisting of very fine grains at their boundaries and coarser elongated grains in the center. The grain boundaries were composed of η-Mg(Al, Zn, Cu)2 eutectic. The associated hardness is quite significant (140 HV0.1). Natural and artificial aging from this state did not show any significant microstructural and hardness evolutions. In contrast, solution heat treatments modified the microstructure by dissolving eutectics and Al3Zr precipitation without significant grain growth. Natural and artificial aging produced interesting hardening: a maximum of 220 HV0.1 was achieved for the T6 temper. The resulting value completely exceeded the hardness of the AW-7075-T6 alloy. This excellent value was attributed to η′ and Al3Zr precipitation without significant grain growth.

Abstract:
This study introduces a family of unique Al–Mn–Cr–Zr-based aluminium alloys illustrated by two ternary and one quaternary variants. The choice of alloy compositions has created a system resistant to solidification cracking while retaining high amount of solutes in solid solution in as-printed condition. Good relative density (~ 99.5%) has been demonstrated along with microstructural study supported by X-ray diffraction to display solidification structure with nanometric precipitate formation in small amounts in as-printed condition. High levels of Mn and Cr produce significant solid solution strengthening reaching hardness of up to 102 HV in as-printed condition. Additionally, the combination of Mn, Cr and Zr is shown to be important to control precipitation strengthening upon direct ageing and coarsening resistance due to slow diffusivity. To elucidate the concept of precipitation strengthening, one set of alloys was aged at 678 K between 0 and 10 h and microhardness results showed that average hardness response reached 130 HV for the quarternary alloy. Abstract:
The demand for high-performance aluminum components drives research into the design of novel alloys that can be processed by laser-based additive manufacturing. In recent years, the addition of grain refiners proved to be an effective strategy to reduce the hot-cracking of high-strength Al alloys. In this study, the solidification and aging behavior of an Al2139 alloy doped with additions of Zr and Ti for L-PBF was investigated. These elements favored the formation of a fine-grained structure free of cracks. The formation of Al3(Zr,Ti) inoculants was predicted by Scheil simulations and observed as cuboidal particles in the center of α-Al grains. The microstructure of the as-built material featured fine and fully equiaxed grains, which appeared comparatively finer at the edge (300–600 nm) and coarser (0.8–2.0 μm) at the center of the molten pools. In both cases, there was evidence of Cu and Mg micro-segregations at the grain boundaries. The microhardness of 109.7 HV0.5 in the as-built state was increased to 186.1 HV0.5 after optimized T4 heat treatment, responsible for the precipitation of many rod-shaped Zr- and Ti-based second phases and quasi-spherical Cu-, Mn-, and Fe-rich particles. Prolonged exposure carried out to simulate high-temperature service caused a drop in microhardness and marked modification of the microstructure, evidenced by the rearrangement and subsequent spheroidization of Cu- and Mg-rich particles at the grain boundaries.

This excerpt is directly relevant to Ekaputra’s scandium-free L-PBF Al-Zr-X alloys, but it reports only the study scope and headline findings, not the detailed creep-test matrix requested. The alloys are binary Al-0.4Zr and ternary Al-0.4Zr-1X (at.%), with X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W. Compressive creep was conducted at 400°C, and every ternary alloy had substantially better creep resistance than binary Al-Zr. The excerpt does not specify applied stresses, test durations, measured secondary creep rates, or rupture outcomes. For thermal aging, the relevant condition is 400°C; long-term exposure caused supersaturated ternary solutes to precipitate as binary Al-X phases. Mn and Cr precipitated faster than V, Mo, and W, while V, Mo, and W remained nearly entirely in solid solution after 2016 hours at 400°C. The excerpt states that ternary-solute strengthening at room temperature did not significantly differ among the five alloys or with aging time, implying a stable contribution despite precipitation, but it provides no numerical hardness values or detailed microstructural measurements. No scandium-containing alloy is described in the tested Ekaputra compositions; Scalmalloy is mentioned only as a commercial comparative example.

The excerpt provides directly relevant evidence for the scandium-free, SLM-processed Griffiths Al–Mg–Zr alloys: Al–3.6Mg–1.2Zr and Al–2.9Mg–2.1Zr (wt%). These alloys were tested in creep at 260 °C, including an 8-hour test and a 168-hour test. In the 8-hour test, as-fabricated material had an approximate threshold stress of 40 MPa, compared with approximately 14 MPa for material previously aged at 260 °C; thus, the as-fabricated condition was more creep-resistant. After 168 hours at 260 °C, the two conditions exhibited nearly identical creep behavior, attributed to coarsening of grain-boundary Al3Zr precipitates during testing. The excerpt does not report numerical minimum creep rates or stress-rupture failure. It also reports short-term yield results at 260 °C: 87 MPa for as-fabricated material versus 24 MPa for peak-aged material. Aging observations include peak aging at 400 °C for 8 hours, producing continuous approximately 2-nm and discontinuous approximately 5-nm Al3Zr precipitates; heating to 500 °C caused most precipitates and oxide particles to disappear. This excerpt provides only partial information relevant to the requested survey and does not document scandium-free Zr-only AlSi10Mg. The reported alloy is AlSi10Mg-Zr-Sc made using pre-alloyed powder, so it should be classified as a Sc-containing comparative alloy rather than a scandium-free result. An original creep experiment was performed at 300 °C for 178 h after peak aging at 300 °C for 96 h, with the figure caption indicating an applied-stress range of 30–106 MPa. The excerpt does not state a measured minimum creep rate, rupture time, or whether rupture occurred. It reports a 108 MPa hardness loss after creep, attributed to strain-accelerated coarsening of the eutectic Si phase, while EBSD showed no appreciable grain growth: grain sizes remained within error, indicating neither recrystallization nor grain growth. The strengthening and creep improvement are associated with secondary Al3(Sc,Zr) nanoparticles, approximately 1.0 ± 0.3 nm in radius. The excerpt contains no long isothermal aging test lasting at least 1000 h at temperatures ≥250 °C. The longest directly stated exposure is the combined 96 h aging plus 178 h creep treatment at 300 °C, and therefore it cannot supply the requested ≥1000 h hardness, microstructural, or mechanical-aging result.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing (AM) can fabricate, repair, and join near-net-shaped components for high-performance engineering applications, including biomedical, energy, and transport sectors. The broader adoption of DED remains constrained by the limited number of alloys available that can be reliably manufactured without imperfections, hence limiting mechanical properties. Here, we designed an Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe AM alloy that can achieve an ultra-fine microstructure (<5 μm), uniform distribution of intermetallics, low residual stress (<32 MPa), and superior mechanical properties in as-built DED components. Compared to DED AlSi10Mg in the as-built state using the same conditions, the yield increased by 70%, and the ultimate tensile strength by 50%. DED-AM involves rapid cooling and complex thermal conditions, which largely influence the property of the final components. Post-characterization cannot capture the time resolved thermal behavior, hence offer limited mechanism-based guide for alloy design. In this study, we develop a novel multimodal characterization methodology for correlative in situ X-ray imaging, X-ray diffraction, and infrared imaging, enabling quantification of the in situ thermal-related behavior, including phase evolution, temperature distribution, and stress accumulation during DED. We elucidated key mechanisms driving the structure refinement and stress development in this alloy. The insights gained into the interplay between alloy composition, thermal-related behavior, and performance under specific AM conditions inform next-generation material design tailored for AM technologies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    To meet the demand for high‐performance lightweight heat‐resistant materials in aerospace and automotive applications, a novel Al‐Fe‐Sc‐Zr heat‐resistant aluminum alloy was fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (L‐PBF). The effects of Mg content (1 wt%, 3 wt%, 5 wt%, and 7 wt%) on formability, microstructure, mechanical properties, and thermal stability were systematically investigated in this study. The results show that this alloy system exhibits excellent processability, with all specimens achieving relative densities above 99%. In terms of mechanical performance, the 5 wt% Mg alloy delivered the optimal strength‐ductility synergy, with an ultimate tensile strength of 566 ± 5 MPa, a yield strength of 510 ± 7 MPa, and an elongation of 7.5% ± 0.5%, outperforming most reported Al‐Fe‐Sc‐Zr alloys. Its yield strength at 300°C remained as high as 107 ± 6 MPa. Mechanistic analysis indicates that Mg addition retards the coarsening of the Al

                    Fe phase, thereby enhancing thermal stability. Overall, 5 wt% Mg is identified as the optimal content that balances formability, mechanical properties, and heat resistance, and this finding provides a crucial basis for the compositional design of this alloy when applied as a lightweight, high‐temperature‐resistant structural material.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a typical additive manufacturing technology that offers significant advantages in the production of complex components. With the rapid heating and cooling characteristics of LPBF, a large amount of solid solution of alloying elements in the matrix can be achieved to form supersaturated solid solutions, thus enhancing the properties of LPBF alloys. For the unique microstructure, the heat treatment process needs to be adjusted accordingly. In this work, a Zr/Sc-modified Al-Mg alloy processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with relatively low cost and good mechanical properties was investigated. The fine microstructure was obtained under rapid solidification conditions. The nanoscale Al3(Sc,Zr) particles precipitated at the molten pool boundary during solidification. These particles, as effective heterogeneous nucleators, further refined the α-Al grains and improved the mechanical properties of the alloy. As a result, the alloy exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure consisting of columnar grains in the center of the molten pool and equiaxed grains at the boundaries. The rapid solidification resulted in the supersaturation of solute atoms in the α-Al matrix, which significantly enhanced the solid solution strengthening effect. With the LPBF processing parameters of a combination of a laser power of 250 W, a laser scanning speed of 833 mm/s, and stripe scanning mode, the tensile strength of the alloy reached 401.4 ± 5.7 MPa, which was significantly higher than that of the cast alloys with aging treatment (281.1 ± 1.3 MPa). The heat treatment promoted the formation of secondary Al3(Sc,Zr), Mn/Mg-rich phases. The ultimate tensile strength and elongation at fracture after aging at 325 °C for 2 h were 536.0 ± 1.7 MPa and 14.8 ± 0.8%, respectively. The results provide insight into the preparation of aluminum alloys with relatively low cost and excellent mechanical properties.

Abstract:
Titanium and its alloys are widely employed in the aerospace industry, and their use will increase in the future. At present, titanium is mainly produced by the Kroll method, but this is expensive and energy-intensive. Therefore, the research of efficient and sustainable methods for its production has become relevant. The present review provides a description of the titanium recycling methods used to produce mostly aeronautical components by additive manufacturing, offering an overview of the actual state of the art in the field. More specifically, this paper illustrates that ilmenite is the main source of titanium and details different metallurgic processes for producing titanium and titanium alloys. The energy consumption required for each production step is also illustrated. An overview of additive manufacturing techniques is provided, along with an analysis of their relative challenges. The main focus of the review is on the current technologies employed for the recycling of swarf. Literature suggests that the most promising ways are the technologies based on severe plastic deformation, such as equal-channel angular pressing, solid-state field-assisted sintering technology-forge, and the Conform process. The latter is becoming established in the field and can replace the actual production of conventional titanium wire. Titanium-recycled powder for additive manufacturing is mainly produced using gas atomization techniques.

Abstract:
<jats:p>To meet the demand for high-performance heat-resistant aluminum alloy conductors in energy transmission, this study systematically explores the effects of synergistic aging and deformation treatment on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and heat resistance of Al-0.04Er-0.08Zr alloy. Through isochronous/isothermal aging, rolling with varying deformation amounts, and microstructural characterization coupled with performance testing, the following findings emerged: 425 °C represents the peak aging temperature, at which a dispersed L12 structure of Al3(Er1−xZrx) composite precipitates with an average size of 4 nm is formed; Dispersed L12 structure Al3(Er1−xZrx) composite precipitation phase achieved an alloy hardness of 49.45 HV and electrical conductivity of 58.68% IACS; the synergistic treatment of peak aging (425 °C) with 60% deformation amount yielded optimal comprehensive properties. After 150 h of isothermal annealing at 350 °C, hardness decreased by less than 5%, and the alloy demonstrated stable service life of approximately 40 years at 227 °C based on Arrhenius model extrapolation. This study reveals the synergistic regulation mechanism between deformation and aging, providing theoretical support and technical reference for developing low-cost, high thermal stability, and high-conductivity aluminum alloys.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this study, the effect of Zr elements on Al–10Ce alloys were investigated in terms of the microstructure, mechanical properties at room and high temperatures, and corrosion resistance. Meanwhile, the finite element simulations on tensile fracture was adopted to explain the fracture process of Al–Ce alloys. Results showed that as Zr content increased from 0.05 to 0.15%, the eutectic Al11Ce3 phase were gradually coarsened. However, further increase in Zr content led to the refinement and homogenization. Meanwhile, a significant transformation in the morphology of eutectic Al11Ce3 from layered to rod-like or bar-like structures happened. Correspondingly, mechanical properties at room temperature such as hardness, tensile strength, and yield strength initially decreased but subsequently increased. The tensile strength and yield strength of the alloys could reach the maximum values of 160 MPa and 96 MPa, respectively, and the elongation of the alloy reached the highest of 14.4%. The yield strength and the tensile strength at high temperature of 300 °C exhibited the highest values of 62.5 Mpa and 74 Mpa, respectively, when the Zr content is 0.05%. Moreover, the corrosion current of the alloys was minimized to 1.158 × 10− 7 µA/cm2 when the content of Zr was 0.05%, which attributed to the observed optimal microstructural characteristics of the Al11Ce3 phase at this concentration. Therefore, it is believed that Al–10Ce–Zr alloys are excellent candidate engineering materials in extreme environment fields.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Conventional precipitation‐strengthened aluminum alloys often lose load‐bearing capacity above approximately 300 °C as matrix softening accompanies precipitate coarsening or dissolution. Solidification‐derived intermetallic architectures offer an alternative route to elevated‐temperature strength through thermally stable lamellar, fibrous, cellular, divorced, or three‐dimensional networks. This review examines heat‐resistant aluminum alloys containing eutectic, near‐eutectic, primary‐phase‐plus‐eutectic, and rapidly solidified eutectic‐like architectures. A manufacturing‐process‐aware framework links alloy chemistry, local thermal history, intermetallic architecture, and defect population across casting, laser powder bed fusion, electron beam powder bed fusion, laser directed energy deposition, and wire arc additive manufacturing. Evidence is categorized into phase stability and hardness retention, instantaneous high‐temperature strength, creep and rupture, fatigue, and component‐scale qualification. Cross‐family comparisons show that refined spacing alone does not ensure heat resistance. Sustained performance also requires sufficient phase fraction, stable morphology and connectivity, matrix strength, interfacial integrity, and tolerance to route‐specific defects. Available studies demonstrate condition‐specific capability within parts of the 300–400 °C range, but the evidence remains uneven and often derives from unmatched test conditions. The resulting family–route–condition framework provides transferable reporting descriptors and qualification priorities without equating thermal stability with structural capability under sustained loading.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The capability for synergistic advancements in both making and shaping afforded by additive manufacturing (AM) enables the flexible production of high-performance components. Boosted by the growing demand for heat-resistant aluminum alloys in the moderate-temperature weight-critical applications, AM of heat-resistant aluminum alloys constitutes a burgeoning field. Although numerous advances have emerged in recent years, there remains a gap in the review literature elucidating the newly-developed alloy systems and critically evaluating the efficacy. This state-of-the-art review presents a detailed overview of recent achievements on the heat-resistant aluminum alloy development. It begins with the introduction of various AM technologies and the pros and cons of each technique are evaluated. The enhancement mechanisms associated with printability and high-temperature properties of AM aluminum alloys are then delineated. Thereafter, the various additively manufactured aluminum alloy systems are discussed with regard to the microstructure, heat resistance and high-temperature performance. An emphasis is put on the powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB) as it has garnered significant attention for heat-resistant aluminum alloys and the vast majority of the current studies are based on this technique. Finally, perspectives are outlined to provide guidance for future research.

Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Al-Ce and Al-Ce-Cr Cast Alloys: Effects of Cr and Solidification Conditions Valid Text Names: 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 1-6', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 6-11', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 11-15', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 15-22', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 22-27', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 27-32', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 32-35', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 35-36' BibTex: @article{junior2026microstructureandmechanical, author = "Júnior, Gueber Elias Mendes Santos and Oliveira, Leonardo Carvalho and Silva, Argos Soares and Leal, Jaderson Rodrigo Silva and Barros, André Santos and Xavier, Marcella Gautê Cavalcante and Spinelli, José Eduardo", title = "Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Al-Ce and Al-Ce-Cr Cast Alloys: Effects of Cr and Solidification Conditions", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Sep", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10918756/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10918756/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

Lightweight Al alloys capable of retaining mechanical performance at elevated temperatures are increasingly relevant for transportation and structural applications. Al-Ce alloys are particularly attractive because of their good castability and thermally stable Ce-containing intermetallics. However, how Cr addition modifies phase formation and mechanical behavior under rapid solidification remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the processing–microstructure–property relationships of Al–13Ce and Al–10Ce–1Cr (wt%) alloys produced by centrifugal solidification (CS), with directional solidification (DS) used for comparison. CS was performed using a stepped Cu mold with bulk diameters of 5–11 mm, and the resulting alloys were characterized by SEM/EDS, XRD, Vickers microhardness, and compression testing. CS produced markedly refined microstructures, with dendritic spacings of approximately 4.0–5.4 µm. The Al–13Ce alloy exhibited a cellular-to-dendritic transition corresponding to samples having smaller diameters, whereas Al–10Ce–1Cr retained a dendritic morphology throughout all conditions. The Cr-containing alloy generally exhibited higher compressive and yield strengths, reaching 282 and 143 MPa, respectively, compared with 253 and 119 MPa for Al–13Ce in the same 11-mm CS condition. The Hollomon analysis revealed a higher strength coefficient (K) but lower strain-hardening exponent (n) for Al–10Ce–1Cr, indicating higher resistance to plastic flow but a reduced strain-hardening capacity, consistent with the presence of primary Al 20 CeCr 2 particles. Overall, the compressive response was governed not only by microstructural refinement but also by phase constitution, intermetallic distribution, and particle/matrix interactions, highlighting the combined roles of alloy chemistry and solidification route in tailoring Al-Ce-based alloys.

Abstract:
Iron-based high-temperature alloys are engineered to withstand extreme conditions, including elevated temperatures, mechanical stress, and corrosive environments. These alloys play a critical role in industries such as aerospace, power generation, and chemical processing, where materials must maintain structural integrity and performance under demanding operational conditions. This review examines recent advancements in iron-based alloys, with a focus on alloying strategies, high-temperature performance, and applications. Traditional approaches—including alloy design, microstructure control, process optimization, and computational modeling—continue to enhance alloy performance. Furthermore, emerging technologies such as high-entropy alloy (HEA) design, additive manufacturing (AM), nanostructured design with nanophase strengthening, and machine learning/artificial intelligence (ML/AI) are revolutionizing the development of iron-based superalloys, creating new opportunities for advanced material applications.

The excerpt provides a directly relevant primary aging exposure for scandium-free laser powder-bed-fusion aluminum alloys: six L-PBF compositions were studied—binary Al-0.4Zr and Al-0.4Zr-1X (at.%), with X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W. The ternary additions were selected as slow-diffusing transition metals, and the nominal composition was 0.4 at.% Zr plus 1 at.% Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W. Aging was performed at 400°C, including exposure for 2016 h, which satisfies the requested minimum duration. The excerpt states that ternary solid solutions decompose during long-term aging to form binary Al-X precipitates. Precipitation is fastest for Mn, followed by Cr, then V, Mo, and W; V, Mo, and W remain almost entirely in solid solution after 2016 h at 400°C. The reported property observation is that the ternary solute’s room-temperature strengthening contribution does not significantly differ among the five alloys or with aging time at 400°C. During 400°C creep testing, all ternary alloys have substantially higher creep resistance than binary Al-Zr. However, these pages do not provide an exact hardness decline, hardness values, or detailed measured before/after property changes. 5.3.    Sample preparation
5.3.1.    Sample designs
Based on work by Pauzon [8], the test coupons were designed with a notch to mark the gas
flow direction, as shown in Figure 31. This enabled the study of three cross sections (XY, XZ
and YZ) in Paper I to verify if there is any effect of gas flow on relative density. Additionally,
the notches were useful for locating the sample edge for microstructural studies when using
electron microscopy. Sample designs were either cubic with 10 mm side or rectangular with
16 mm height, 8 mm length and 8 mm width.





Figure 31 Sample with notch for manufacturing cubes for microstructural studies [48]
5.3.2.    Metallography
Depending on the analysis to be conducted, several planes were studied. For DOE samples to
measure density, all three XY, XZ and YZ planes were studied for samples produced in EOS

                                          36M100 machine and XZ, and XY planes were studied for samples produced in EOS M290
machine. For heat-treated samples, only XZ and XY planes were characterised. The samples
were cut using a precision saw and mounted on polyfast resin (from Struers, Denmark). The
samples were ground and polished based on a self-developed procedure. The procedure can be
found elsewhere [46], [48], [126]. It can be summarised as follows
o  Grinding of samples starting with SiC-foil #240 or #320 to make the samples flat
o  Grinding progressively with finer grit foils till SiC-foil #4000
o  Polishing with 1 µm diamond paste with 20 N load 3-5 min and 15 N 3-5 min
o  Final polishing with OP-S suspension 15 N 1-2 min (with suspension) and 15 N 2 min with
   water only

Etching of aluminium samples was not needed for revealing microstructure as back-scatter
mode was used for most electron microscopy analyses with good results. OP-S suspension
provides slight etching too. Selected samples were chemically etched for optical microscopy
for which Keller’s reagent was used. The recipe was comprised of 95 ml water, 2.5 ml HNO3,
1.5 ml HCl and 1 ml HF. Etching was conducted by directly dipping the sample into the etchant
for 8-10 s followed by dipping in water and then cleaning with ethanol. The samples for
transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were prepared by preparing thin foils (0.1 mm) along
the XZ plane of the sample followed by punching to discs of 3 mm diameter. These discs were
then twin-jet electropolished using Struers Tenupol 5 machine with freshly prepared Struers
A2 electrolyte at 243 K and 15V. The samples for synchrotron studies were prepared using
plasma focused ion beam (FIB) using a Xe+ ion at TESCAN, Czech Republic. Plasma FIB was
used  to avoid  grain boundary contamination of  the aluminium, which  is common  in
conventional Ga-FIB [127], [128]. The as-printed samples were polished along the XZ plane
up to the mirror finish (1 µm polishing step). This was then followed by the FIB lift-out
produced using a TESCAN AmberX plasma-FIB SEM at TESCAN, Czech Republic.
5.4.   CALPHAD simulation and precipitation modelling
The simulations conducted for alloy design and simulation of possible precipitation response
were conducted using Thermo-Calc software provided by Thermo-Calc software AB, Sweden.
For the thesis, Thermo-Calc 2019-22 versions of the software were used depending on the latest
version available. The material databases for aluminium alloys were TCAL6-8 databases [100]
from Thermo-Calc AB and COST507 open CALPHAD database [129]. For precipitation
modelling  calculations,  mobility  databases MOBAL5-6 were used. The  use  of  these
simulations has been limited to act as a guide to alloy design due to the unavailability of studied
thermodynamic  databases (Al-Mn-Cr-Zr  based) and  the  limited  development  of non-
equilibrium reactions. Paper VIII elaborates on the benefits of having a database explaining
the effects of Cr on Mn-rich precipitates which could not be done with available TCAL
databases.
5.5.    Heat treatments
All the heat treatments at >523 K were conducted in a pre-heated resistance coil furnace with
a secondary thermocouple close to the sample (<5 mm) to ensure temperature control within
±2 K close to the sample. The heat treatments at <523 K were conducted in a convection-heated
oven with a similar setup for a secondary thermocouple to ensure temperature control.

5.6.1.    Optical microscopy
Light optical microscopy (LOM) analysis was conducted on a ZEISS Axioscope 7 instrument.
The microscope is equipped with an automated stage that can capture stitched images of larger
sample sections. For large-area analysis to measure the relative density of samples, a 10x
optical zoom was used, providing a resolution of 0.4 µm/pixel. This resolution could resolve
defects up to ~1 µm (~6 pixels) with reasonable accuracy. The image analysis to obtain relative

was conducted on a ZEISS stereo discovery.V20 microscope. The SOM was used for the
fractography of specimens from tensile and bending fatigue testing.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is a characterization technique that can help to study the
structure of materials at several length scales. Based on which electron imaging is being done,
the contrast could reveal information about the material [130]. For this thesis, backscatter
electron (BSE) imaging was employed primarily. The benefit of BSE imaging is that atomic
contrast can be seen as grey contrast of images.

## 3. ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000019)

               Coarsening- and creep behavior of supersaturated Al-Zr-X
         (X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, W) alloys processed by laser powder-bed fusion

     Clement N. Ekaputraa, Ekin Senvardarlia, Christian Leinenbachb,c, David C. Dunanda

         a Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208, USA

        b Empa, Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, Dübendorf 8600, Switzerland

                 c École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Laboratory for Photonic Materials and
                                   Characterization, Lausanne 1015, Switzerland


Abstract

We characterize the high-temperature microstructural evolution and creep properties of binary
Al-0.4Zr and ternary Al-0.4Zr-1X (at.%) alloys fabricated by laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF),
where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W are slow-diffusing transition metals added for solid-solution
strengthening. All alloys contain strengthening L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates which form during
aging at 400°C. In the as-fabricated alloys, the ternary solute is nearly all in solid solution in the
Mn- and Cr-containing alloys, and partially in solution in the V-, Mo-, and W-containing alloys,
but still in amounts well beyond the equilibrium solubility limit for these elements. Solid
solutions of the ternary solutes decompose during long-term aging at 400°C to form binary Al-X
precipitates. The relative rates of precipitation of these elements are consistent with their relative
diffusivities in Al: the precipitation rate is fastest for Mn, followed by Cr, then V, Mo, and W
(the latter three elements remain almost entirely in solid solution after 2016 h exposure at
400°C). Nevertheless, the strengthening contribution from the ternary solute at room temperature
does not significantly differ among the five studied alloys or as a function of aging time at
400°C, indicating a stable strengthening contribution from Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W in Al. During
creep deformation at 400°C, all ternary alloys show significantly higher creep resistance than a
binary Al-Zr alloy. Furthermore, their creep resistance is comparable to those of additively-
manufactured alloys with significantly higher volume fractions of strengthening phases.1. Introduction

Aluminum-based alloys processed by laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing
often have unique, non-equilibrium microstructures due to the fast cooling rates (>105-106 K/s)
inherent to the L-PBF process [1]. One important aspect of these non-equilibrium
microstructures is the ability to achieve extended solid solutions well beyond their maximum
equilibrium solubility [2]. As a result, Al-based alloys designed for additive manufacturing can
be more heavily alloyed than those designed for conventional, near-equilibrium solidification
(such as casting), and by extension often display much enhanced mechanical properties due to
greater solid-solution or secondary-precipitation strengthening [1].

One important example of such alloys are L12-strengthened Al alloys, where high amounts of
L12-forming elements (Sc, Zr, Ti) beyond their maximum solid solubilities in Al promote both
printability and large strengthening responses during secondary aging [3, 4]. Two prominent
commercial examples of such alloys are Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Scalmalloy) [5] and Al-Mg-Zr
(Addalloy) [6] alloys, but many similar alloys exist in the literature (e.g., Al-Mn-Mg-Sc-Zr [7],
Al-Mn-Cr-Zr [8], Al-Cu-Mn-Zr [9], Al-Cu-Sc-Zr [10], Al-Zn-Mg-Sc-Zr [11]), where high
amounts of additional alloying elements (Mg, Mn, Cu, Cr, Zn) beyond their equilibrium
solubility limits provide additional solid-solution or precipitation strengthening. In this work, we
focus on the high-temperature solid-solution strengthening effect of five transition metals in
ternary Al-Zr-X systems, for design of Al alloys with excellent high-temperature mechanical
properties.

Here, we study the addition of Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W to the Al-Zr system. Among the various
solid-solution strengthening elements in Al, these five elements provide some of the highest
solid-solution strengthening increments per at.% added [1, 12]. This is due to their large lattice
misfit in Al: from first-principles calculations [12], a 75-125 MPa yield-strength increment can
be expected from 1 at.% addition of these elements, as opposed to <25 MPa/at.% from Mg or Zn.
However, the low equilibrium solid solubility of these elements in Al limits the amount that can
be added under conventional processes, but the rapid solidification rates provided by L-PBF AM
enables much higher amounts of these elements to be added in supersaturated solid solution,
increasing their possible solution strengthening effect. For example, Al-4.5Mn-1.3Mg-0.79Sc-
0.74Zr (wt.%) [13] and Al-5.0Mn-0.8Cr-0.6Zr (wt.%) [8] alloys processed by L-PBF fully retain
their respective amounts of Mn and Cr in solid solution after L-PBF, leading to high strength in
the as-fabricated state. Earlier work in the rapid solidification literature on the binary Al-Mn, Al-
Cr, Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-W systems [14] suggests that 2.2% Mn, 0.94% Cr, 0.53% V, 0.18%
Mo, and 0.18% W (at.%), respectively, is retained in solid solution for cooling rates of 103-104
K/s. Similar studies show as much as 2.0 at.% V [15], 2.45 at.% Mo [16], and 1.0 at.% W [17]
can be obtained for higher cooling rates (>105 K/s), which are more similar to the cooling rates
expected in L-PBF [1], suggesting high amounts of possible solid-solution strengthening from
alloys containing these elements.

Furthermore, previous experimental work indicates that slow-diffusing solute elements can also
provide resistance to creep deformation at high temperatures. The creep strengthening effect of
Mn solutes have been widely studied. In a study by Farkoosh et al. [18], the presence of just 0.5at.% Mn in an Al-0.5Mn-0.02Si alloy reduced creep strain rates at 300°C by 5-6 orders of
magnitude when compared to pure Al. In the same study, the dislocation creep threshold stress of
an Al-0.5Mn-0.09Zr-0.05Er-0.05Si alloy was more than three times higher than that of a similar
Al-0.11Zr-0.005Er (at.%) alloy without Mn. Similar results have been found in cast Al-Ce-Mn
[19] and L-PBF processed Al-Mn-Sc [20] alloys. In all these studies, it is proposed that attractive
forces exerted by slow-diffusing Mn atoms slow the climb of dislocations, reducing creep strain
rates. More generally, other slow-diffusing elements, such as Fe [21], also improve creep
resistance, while fast-diffusing elements such as Cu, Zn, and Bi [22] provide no creep
strengthening and may even increase creep strain rates.

A natural question, then, is whether solutes which diffuse even slower than Mn in Al – such as
Cr, V, Mo, and W – also have a stronger creep strengthening effect than Mn when in solid
solution in Al. The diffusivity of Mn at 400 °C is 9 x 10-19 m2/s, that of Cr is two orders of
magnitude lower (1.3 x 10-21 m2/s), and those of V, Mo, and W are 5-6 orders of magnitude
lower than Mn (5 x 10-24, 5 x 10-23, and 5 x 10-23 m2/s, respectively) [23]. Several previous
studies have examined the effects of slow diffusing elements (Cr, V, Mo, W) on the creep
resistance of Zr-containing cast Al alloys [24-28], but only in small amounts (<0.1 at.%) as the
achievable solubility of these elements in cast alloys is quite low. Earlier studies have reported
improved creep rupture life in more concentrated, rapidly-solidified, binary Al-Cr, -V, -Mo, or -
W alloys [14], but do not report the secondary creep strain rates in these alloys. Thus, there is a
gap in the literature on the creep properties of rapidly-solidified Al alloys strengthened by stable,
extended solid solutions.

Here, we study six L-PBF processed Al alloys: a binary Al-0.4Zr alloy, and five ternary Al-
0.4Zr-1X (at.%) alloys, where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W are all slow-diffusing transition metal
elements. The 1 at.% concentration of the ternary solute is selected based on the above literature
suggesting that this amount could be retained in solid solution for rapidly-solidified binary Al-X
alloys, and kept constant between alloys to isolate effects of the solute itself on microstructure
and mechanical properties. We focus first on the as-fabricated, rapidly-solidified microstructure
of these alloys to determine if supersaturated solid solutions of these elements can be achieved.
Then, we evaluate the stability of these solid solutions during aging at temperatures >400°C, and
the effect of any precipitation on the room-temperature microhardness. Lastly, we study the
effect of these alloying elements on compressive creep properties at 400°C, comparing the effect
of alloying element and aging condition.2. Experimental procedures

Six alloy compositions were prepared: a binary Al-0.4Zr (at.%) alloy, and five ternary Al-0.4Zr-
1X (at.%) alloys, where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W. For brevity, these alloys will be referred to as
Al-Zr and Al-Zr-X alloys. Bi

Abstract:
With development of present energy-saving society, lightweight and green development in the automotive and aerospace industries have put forward urgent demands for heat-resistant cast aluminum alloys. Present cast aluminum alloys are of lightweight and have excellent mechanical properties when serving in ambient environment. However, when serving at temperatures of 200–300 ℃ or even higher, the alloys inevitably soften and the high-temperature mechanical properties decline rapidly, hardly meeting the requirements for high-performance equipments. This paper summarizes the development process of classic heat-resistant aluminum alloys, especially the microstructural characteristics of heat-resistant cast aluminum alloys in the past decade, and reviews the current microstructure tuning strategies of heat-resistant aluminum alloys from the aspects of intrinsic heat resistance of the second phases, phase interface modification, diffusion-controlled phase transition, grain boundary stabilization and composite material design. Finally, we propose the prospects for the future development of heat-resistant aluminum alloys.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The samples of the Al–15Fe (mass%) binary alloy that were additively manufactured by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) were exposed to intermediate temperatures (300 and 500 °C), and the thermally induced variations in their microstructural characteristics were investigated. The L-PBF-manufactured sample was found to have a microstructure comprising a stable θ-Al13Fe4 phase localized around melt-pool boundaries and several spherical metastable Al6Fe-phase particles surrounded by a nanoscale α-Al/Al6Fe cellular structure in the melt pools. The morphology of the θ phase remained almost unchanged even after 1000 h of exposure at 300 °C. Moreover, the nanoscale α-Al/Al6Fe cellular structure dissolved in the α-Al matrix; this was followed by the growth (and nucleation) of the spherical Al6Fe-phase particles and the precipitation of the θ phase. Numerous equiaxed grains were formed in the α-Al matrix during the thermal exposure, which led to the formation of a relatively homogenous microstructure. The variations in these microstructural characteristics were more pronounced at the higher investigated temperature of 500 °C.</jats:p>

The excerpt provides the Sisco et al. 2023 findings for LPBF Al-Ce-Mn, but it does not state the alloy’s exact bulk Ce/Mn composition, nor does it report hardness or strength measurements. The specimen was heat treated isothermally at 400 °C for 1000 h. Relative to the as-fabricated condition, which contained FCC Al, Al20Mn2Ce, and Al11Ce3, heat treatment produced additional Al6Mn, Al12Mn, and Al51Mn7Ce4 phases. The refined heat-treated phase fractions were FCC Al (50.9 ± 0.04 wt.%), Al20Mn2Ce (1.4 ± 0.02 wt.%), Al11Ce3 (8.2 ± 0.01 wt.%), Al6Mn (17.3 ± 0.04 wt.%), Al12Mn (5.5 ± 0.04 wt.%), and Al51Mn7Ce4 (16.7 ± 0.03 wt.%). Thus, Al20Mn2Ce decomposed during exposure, with the text indicating that particles in the eutectic region followed the same pathway as those in the melt-pool-boundary region. Al11Ce3 was treated as stable because it is an equilibrium phase at 400 °C and was not expected to decompose. The excerpt contains no information about the requested comparative LPBF Al-15Fe Wang 2022 treatment at 300 °C for 1000 h, or the Al-Mn-Cr-Zr Mehta et al. 2023 treatment at 350 °C for 1000 h and associated hardness changes.

                                                                             1 Load shuffling during creep deformation of an additively manufactured AlCuMnZr alloy


Richard A. Michi1, Sumit Bahl1, Christopher M. Fancher1, Kevin Sisco2, Lawrence F. Allard1,

Ke An3, Dunji Yu3, Ryan R. Dehoff4, Alex Plotkowski1, Amit Shyam1*


1Materials Science and Technology Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN

2Department of Mechanical, Aerospace, and Biomedical Engineering, University of Tennessee,

Knoxville, TN

3Neutron Scattering Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN

4Manufacturing Science Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN


*Corresponding author: A. Shyam (email: [email redacted]; phone: +18652414841)


Abstract

The high-temperature deformation behavior of an additively manufactured Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy is

evaluated in the as-fabricated and heat-treated states using traditional ex-situ and in-situ neutron

diffraction creep experiments performed at 300 °C. The dominant reinforcement phase in the alloy,

θ-Al2Cu, despite its high volume fraction of ~10%, does not provide load transfer strengthening
during creep deformation. Instead, the lattice strain evolution suggests a new mechanism we term

“load shuffling” wherein the initial load is transferred away from precipitate-free zones along the

grain boundaries where most of the θ-Al2Cu particles are located to precipitate-strengthened grain
interiors. Notwithstanding the lack of load transfer strengthening, the as-fabricated AM Al-Cu-

Mn-Zr alloy still possesses improved creep resistance at 300 °C relative to a cast alloy with similar

composition. The proposed load shuffling mechanism explains the lack of observed L12-Al3Zr
strengthening at 300 °C and helps identify several strategies for improvement of elevated-

temperature mechanical response of AM Al alloys.


Keywords: Additive manufacturing, neutron diffraction, creep, aluminum alloys, load transfer





                                                                             21.  Introduction

By utilizing the unique processing conditions associated with additive manufacturing (AM), it may

be possible to design novel high-temperature Al alloys for use in the 200–450 °C temperature

range, where traditional Al alloys lose their strength and consequently, heavier and/or more

expensive Ti alloys and steels are utilized [1]. As the range and scope of Al alloys which are

suitable for AM processing continues to grow [2–4], several recent studies have begun to realize

their potential for high-temperature performance.


Some examples of new Al alloys laser powder bed processed for elevated temperature applications

follow. Binary AM Al-Fe alloys with 2–15 wt.% Fe have been reported which are strengthened by

the nanometric metastable Al6Fe phase. These alloys maintain their strengths after hundreds of
hours aging at 300 °C, and the Al-15Fe alloy exhibits a compressive yield strength of 340 MPa at

300 °C [5–8]. In another binary alloy, AM Al-5.7Ni, a yield strength at 300 °C of 137 ± 2 MPa

was reported, which is 66 MPa higher than AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg at the same temperature [9,10].

Alloys containing several wt.% Ce which promotes formation of Ce-rich strengthening phases

upon solidification have also been developed, including Al-10Ce-8Mn [11], Al-9Cu-6Ce-(1Zr)

[12,13], Al-11Ce-7Mg and Al-15Ce-9Mg [14], Al-11Ce-3Ni-1Mn [15], and Al-8Ce-0.2Sc-0.1Zr

(laser-surface-remelted) [16]. The inherent coarsening resistance of the Ce-rich phases due to low

solubility and diffusivity of Ce in the Al matrix [17] contributes to the strength retention of these

alloys after hundreds of hours aging at 300–400 °C and, combined with microstructural refinement

from AM processing, contributes to elevated temperature yield strengths consistently superior to

those of AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg [9] and Scalmalloy®, two common alloys used for AM of Al.


Despite the lightweighting potential of these high-temperature alloys, creep deformation studies

which are critical for long-lifetime component design are not common. There have been a handful

of creep studies at 150–300 °C on the widely used AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg alloy [9,18–22]. During

creep deformation, the cellular eutectic Si network rapidly coarsens, which contributes to a

decrease in the creep resistance. However, the alloy does have comparable creep resistance at 300

°C to cast high-temperature alloys such as Al-10Ce-5Ni [23] and Al-7Ce-9Mg [24], suggesting

that despite its lack of microstructural coarsening resistance, AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg may still be an

acceptable candidate for use at ~300 °C. The 260 °C creep resistance of AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg is

                                                                             3similar to as-fabricated AM Al-2.9Mg-2.1Zr, which is strengthened by L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates
and Mg in solid solution [25]. However, the creep threshold stress of the AM Al-Mg-Zr alloy drops

dramatically from ~40 MPa in the as-fabricated state to ~14 MPa after either a peak aging

treatment at 400 °C or in-situ aging during creep at 260 °C [25]. The drop in creep strength was

attributed to grain boundary sliding enabled by the coarsening and subsequent reduced pinning

effectiveness of grain boundary particles and the prevalence of refined grains on the order of ~0.8

μm  in  diameter. A high volume  fraction (~35%)  of submicron and  coarsening-resistant

intermetallic phases contributed to the excellent creep resistance recently reported in a Al-11Ce-

3Ni-1Mn alloy at 300–400 °C [15]. This alloy has creep resistance at 300 °C approaching that of

advanced powder metallurgy Al alloys [26] and is a likely template for design of future creep-

resistant AM Al alloys.


Despite these existing creep studies, there is still a need for greater understanding of how common

microstructural features in AM Al alloys such as refined grains, dispersoids, precipitates and melt

pool boundaries affect the creep behavior. The present contribution deals with another common

microstructural feature of the high-temperature AM Al alloys mentioned thus far: a high volume

fraction (> ~10%) of reinforcing phase. This volume fraction of reinforcement is expected to result

in load transfer to the harder reinforcing particles from the softer Al matrix during creep

deformation [15,27–30]. Although load transfer has been inferred in many of the papers cited

herein, to our knowledge it has never been directly measured in an AM aluminum alloy. For a cast

Al-Cu alloy, it was recently revealed through in-situ neutron diffraction that a strengthening θ'-

Al2Cu phase shoulders a significant portion of the load during 300 °C creep deformation [31]
which was similar to the mechanical response of the same phase under ambient temperature

monotonic deformation [32]. Load transfer during creep of microstructurally similar Al metal

matrix composites has been directly measured in situ using neutron diffraction [33–35]. Results

from these studies indicate that the load transfer response is highly sensitive to reinforcement

volume fraction, coherency, crystallography, and morphology. For example, 0.5 μm diameter SiC

whiskers provide significantly higher load transfer compared to similar volume fractions of 20 μm

SiC particles [33].

situ neutron diffraction creep tests to explain the effects of load transfer on the high-temperature

performance of AM Al alloys. The results are linked to the alloy microstructure as evaluated on

multiple length scales across several different heat treatment conditions. Recent studies have

shown that the chosen AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy possesses a favorable combination of room

temperature yield strength (279 MPa) and ductility (11%) in the as-fabricated state [36,37]. The

alloy is heat-treatable, and the room-temperature yield strength can be further improved to 341

MPa with a 300 °C, 200 h heat treatment with no penalty in ductility [37]. A high volume fraction,
