                                               I.    INTRODUCTION



      With the expansion of additive manufacturing (AM), there is a desire for materials

that are lightweight, low cost, and can be used in high temperature environments, such as

in engines or aerospace applications. Many high-temperature aluminum alloys face issues

during AM production such as solidification cracking [1,2,3] and high cost [3]. Al-Ce

alloys are being explored due to their outstanding printability [4], the relative low cost of

cerium [5], and thermal stability [6]. Al-10Ce (wt.%) is a near-eutectic binary alloy with a

narrow solidification range. To determine the feasibility of AM Al-Ce alloys in high

temperature applications, the creep property will be evaluated at homologous temperatures

between 0.6 and 0.75. By testing such a binary alloy, the effect of cerium on the mechanical

properties of AM aluminum alloy can be  isolated. The microstructure, mechanical

properties, and creep results will also be compared to cast Al-10Ce to explore the effect

AM has on the material.


      While aluminum alloys are lightweight, low cost, and corrosion resistant, their

microstructural stability and high temperature strength degrade rapidly with increasing

temperature and over time, limiting their high-temperature applications [3]. Currently, few

commercial high-temperature aluminum alloys are available [3]. One method of increasing

aluminum’s high temperature stability is through solid solution strengthening by alloying

with solutes such as Mg or Mn, or through precipitation strengthening by alloying with

rare earth elements such as Sc or Zr [3]. Sc and Zr have been used as alloying elements to

increase strength through precipitation and prevent intermetallic coarsening during aging

[6]. Cerium has been shown to have a similar effect on the temperature stability [7] at a                                                                       2


lower cost, between 80-100 times less expensive than other rare earth elements [5,8]. Die

cast eutectic Al-Ce alloy has a σ0.2 = 50 MPa and a UTS = 152 MPa [9], maintaining 80%

of its room-temperature mechanical properties at 240 °C. The intermetallic phase (Al11Ce3)

precipitates dendritically in a “Chinese script” morphology and provides strengthening [7].

Although Ce has been shown to improve thermal stability of Al alloys, it remains unknown

what effect it may have on the mechanical properties of AM Al alloys, given their refined

grain structure [10] and increased dislocation density [11].


      Cerium lends thermal stability to aluminum as an alloying element by nature of its

interaction with the fcc α-Al matrix. Al11Ce3 forms at the eutectic temperature of 644.5°C

and is arranged geometrically within the α-Al matrix [12]. The Al11Ce3 phase acts as

reinforcement, with a hardness of 350 HV compared to the aluminum matrix at 35 HV

[12]. However, alloying with cerium alone improves the strength of the alloy very little.

The benefit of cerium comes from the low diffusivity and solubility of cerium in aluminum.

Cerium has a diffusion coefficient about 4 orders of magnitude lower than Mg, Si, Zn, or

Cu [13, 14, 15]. The solid-state solubility of cerium in aluminum is near-zero, reaching an

estimated maximum of 0.01 wt.% at the eutectic temperature [8].


      The uncertainty of the effect of localized heating and repeated melting and

solidification in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) on the behavior of metallic alloys limits

the materials currently available for AM [4]. Primarily, only AlSi10Mg is certified for

metal AM as other commercial Al alloys are prone to solidification cracking [1,2].

However, the mechanical properties of near-eutectic Al-Si compositions cannot compete

with 2xxx or 7xxx series aluminum alloys [16]. While AlSi10Mg produced by LPBF shows

improved creep resistance compared to  its  traditionally cast counterpart, the  stress

4.1. Solute supersaturation in L-PBF Al-Zr-X alloys

Supersaturated solid solutions of Zr and the ternary alloying element X (Cr, V, Mo, and W) were
observed in both the binary Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys. These solid solutions were
observed directly via APT analyses (Fig. 5), and indirectly via SEM (Fig. 4) and electrical
conductivity analyses (Fig. 8). These supersaturated solid solutions are achieved in the L-PBF
Al-Zr-Cr, -V, -Mo, and -W alloys in concentrations beyond what was attainable in the arc-melted
alloys, due to the faster solidification rates in L-PBF..

The Al-Zr-Mn and -Cr alloys did not show obvious primary precipitates, unlike the Al-Zr-V, -
Mo, and -W alloys, which is attributed to the varying solidification intervals of these alloys. In
the Al-Zr-Mn alloy, a supersaturated solid solution was achieved in both the arc-melted and L-
PBF processed alloys. In the binary Al-Mn system, the solidification interval is quite small (1°C
for 1 at.% Mn, calculated via Thermo-Calc, TCAL8 database), and as a result little undercooling
is required to trap Mn in solution. This is consistent with the high amounts of Mn in solid
solution observed in the arc-melted Al-Zr-Mn alloy, as well as in other studies where as much as
~2 at.% Mn was retained in solution. For Al-Cr, the solidification interval is much larger (101°C
for 1 at.% Cr), which is qualitatively consistent with little solute supersaturation in the arc-
melted alloy, but much greater amounts in the L-PBF processed alloy. For Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-
W, the solidification intervals are even larger (315, 205, and 375°C for 1 at.% V, Mo, W
respectively). In the L-PBF process, it is well-established that the solidification velocity and
cooling rates are lowest at the meltpool boundary, and fastest at the center of the meltpool [6].
As a result, the slower cooling rates at the meltpool boundaries are insufficient to fully suppress
primary Al-X precipitation in the V-, Mo-, and W-containing alloys, but the faster cooling rates
near the center of the meltpool are sufficient, as observed for primary Al3Zr precipitates in many
other Al-Zr based alloys [6, 7, 46].

These observations are consistent with previous results in the rapid solidification and L-PBF
literature. Fedorov and Elagin [14] studied supersaturation in binary Al-X alloys (the same
elements as studied here), where mm-size granules were cooled from the melt at a rate of 103-104
K/s. In their study, the maximum achievable solute supersaturation in various binary Al-X alloys
was 2.2% Mn, 0.94% Cr, 0.53% V, 0.18% Mo, and 0.18% W (at.%). For our Al-Zr-Mn and Al-
Zr-Cr alloys, the high supersaturation of Mn and Cr is consistent with the extended solubility for
these elements observed by the above authors [14] at 103-104 K/s. Other researchers have
studied rapid solidification of these binary Al-Mn [47] and Al-Cr [48-50] systems, and observed
even greater extended solutions (up to 5 wt.%) for both Mn and Cr. Mn and Cr have also been
studied in L-PBF processed alloys [8, 13, 51] and extended solid solutions of up to 4.5 wt.% Mn
and 3 wt.% Cr have been observed in L-PBF. In rapidly solidified Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-W alloys
cooled at a rate of 105-106 K/s (similar to L-PBF), as much as 2 at.% V [15], 1.3 at.% Mo [16],
and 1.0 at.% W [17], which is consistent with the microstructures of the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W
alloys at the center of the meltpool. However, the cooling rates at the meltpool boundary may be
insufficient to trap the amounts of V, Mo, and W added to these Al-Zr-X alloys. In Al-Mn-Sc
alloys with similar microstructure, the presence of primary Mn-rich intermetallic precipitatesnear the meltpool boundary can initiate failure there [52]. In these Al-Zr-X based alloys, it may
therefore be desirable to lower the ternary solute content for similar reasons, but more studies are
required to quantify the effect of solute content on mechanical properties.

5. Conclusions

Advancement to the pre-established Al-Mn-Cr-Zr family of alloys tailored for PBF-LB process has
been shown. The new variants with increased Zr content and addition of Mg showed high as-
printed hardness of 132 HV in the most alloyed version (alloy F). Addition of Mg alone caused
solidiﬁcation cracking (alloy E) and was balanced by increasing Zr content (alloy F). As a result,
heavy grain reﬁnement with bimodal grain distribution is caused leading to tentative isotropic
properties. Direct ageing response reveal faster precipitation kinetics than previously established
in alloy C. The amount of hardening via direct ageing in alloy F was similar to alloy C (40 HV)
making the peak hardness reach 172 HV after ageing 623 K 24 h and 648 K 8 h, which suggests

Our hypothesis is that controlling the nucleation barrier for certain phases within the

solidification microstructure may trigger specific transformation pathways during heat treatment

of AM alloys. The activation energy for precipitate nucleation is a function of interfacial energy (
γ), volumetric driving force (ΔGv), and long-range strain energy (ΔGs) for a given matrix
composition and the initial microstructure. We postulate that the above theoretical framework

can be extended to the heterogenous characteristics (compositions and phases) in AM

microstructures by considering every voxel* as locally homogeneous and independent. This

assumption has a caveat that the nucleation and growth of a new phase in each voxel does not

affect thermodynamics of nearby voxels. We evaluate the validity of this assumption in a model

Al-Ce-Mn alloy.

Background on the Al-Ce-Mn System
The Al-Ce-Mn system has been observed to have different decomposition pathways based upon

its initial solidified state. In cast Al-9.0Ce-6.2Mn (wt. %), Yang et al. [25] observed

solidification of the metastable Al20Mn2Ce phase over the equilibrium Al10Mn2Ce phase under
certain conditions. Yang’s calculations showed that differences in solid-liquid interfacial energy

result in a competition between homogeneous nucleation of the two intermetallic phases as a

function of undercooling in the liquid. The Al20Mn2Ce phase preferentially nucleated when the
liquid undercooling is high. Additionally, Yang et al. observed that the Al20Mn2Ce phase
decomposed into the ternary equilibrium phase Al10Mn2Ce after heat treatment at 400°C.

In additive manufacturing of Al-Ce-Mn, Plotkowski et al. [26] observed the suppression of the

Al10Mn2Ce phase and a mix of non-equilibrium Al20Mn2Ce particles at the melt pool boundary
where R is low and G is high. Eutectic solidification of FCC Al and Al20Mn2Ce was found near
the center of melt pools where R is high, and G is low. These two regions, while containing the

same phases (FCC Al, Al11Ce3, and Al20Mn2Ce) decomposed into two different microstructures,
which will be further discussed later.

2.1 Materials and Manufacturing
An Al-10Ce-8Mn (wt.%) [or Al-2.2Ce-4.5Mn (at. %)], alloy was produced by melting and

mixing of raw materials in a 250 kg SiC crucible using an argon cover gas. Cast ingots were

nitrogen gas atomized to produce powders. The powder was sieved for a 20-63 µm size

distribution. AM was performed using a Concept Laser M2 laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF)

system. A more detailed description of the alloy production and composition is found by

Plotkowski et al [26]. There is notably slight Si contamination in the alloy as measured by

inductively coupled plasma. The silicon content is measured to be less than 0.1 wt.%. AM

samples were heat treated in air at 400 °C for up to 1000 h. The heat-treated samples were air

cooled to room temperature.

2.2 Synchrotron X-ray Diffraction
High resolution X-ray diffraction patterns were collected from samples with different heat

treatment conditions at Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) at the Advanced Photon Source

(APS) 11-BM high resolution powder diffraction beamline through the rapid-access mail-in

program. Bulk AM samples were made into filings by filing with a diamond file. Although

efforts were made during the filing to reduce the amount of cold work by this process, the main

goal of these measurements are only relevant for the phase identification. Data were collected

between 0.5° and 50° 2𝜃. A calibrated wavelength of 𝜆 = 0.457927 Å was used. The samples

filings were loaded in 1mm diameter Kapton tubes. Additional details about 11-BM can be found

from Wang et al. [31].

package [32] to extract phase fractions and to refine crystallographic parameters associated with

the Al51Mn7Ce4 phase. The Al51Mn7Ce4 phase identified here was modeled after the

Abstract:
Diesel engines in heavy-duty vehicles are predicted to maintain a stable presence in the future due to the difficulty of electrifying heavy trucks, mine equipment, and railway cars. This trend encourages the effort to develop new aluminum alloy systems with improved performance at diesel engine conditions of elevated temperature and stress combinations to reduce vehicle weight and, consequently, CO2 emissions. Aluminum alloys need to provide adequate creep resistance at ~300 °C and room-temperature tensile properties better than the current commercial aluminum alloys used for powertrain applications. The studies for improving creep resistance for aluminum casting alloys indicate that their high-temperature stability depends on the formation of high-density uniform dispersoids with low solid solubility and low diffusivity in aluminum. This review summarizes three generations of diesel engine aluminum alloys and focuses on recent work on the third-generation dispersoid-strengthened alloys. Additionally, new trends in developing creep resistance through the development of alloy systems other than Al-Si-based alloys, the optimization of manufacturing processes, and the use of thermal barrier coatings and composites are discussed. New progress on concepts regarding the thermal stability of rapidly solidified and nano-structured alloys and on creep-resistant alloy design via machine learning-based algorithms is also presented.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study employs a combined approach of theoretical calculations and experimental validation to systematically optimize the alloy composition, aiming to mitigate the hot cracking susceptibility of an Al-3.0Ce-xCa-yMn alloy in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processing. Through advanced characterization techniques such as electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and mechanical property testing, the intrinsic relationship between microstructure and mechanical performance was thoroughly elucidated. Computational results revealed that the addition of Ca significantly lowered the eutectic precipitation temperature, thereby effectively reducing the hot cracking tendency while maintaining a stable volume fraction of the Al11(Ce, Ca)3 phase. The optimal mass fractions of calcium (Ca) and manganese (Mn) were determined to be 0.8% and 1.9%, respectively. Microstructural characterization indicates that the alloy consisted of an α-Al matrix embedded with Al-Ce-Ca ternary eutectic compounds, and nanoscale Al6Mn spherical precipitates were uniformly distributed within the matrix. Mechanical property evaluations demonstrated that the Al-3Ce-0.8Ca-1.9Mn alloy exhibited an outstanding balance of strength and ductility at both room and elevated temperatures, with room temperature yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation values of 321 ± 15 MPa, 429 ± 8 MPa, and 10.9 ± 2.3%, respectively. This exceptional performance was attributed to a synergistic combination of multiple strengthening mechanisms including eutectic structure-induced strengthening, grain boundary strengthening due to ultrafine grains, and dislocation pinning strengthening caused by nano-sized Al6Mn precipitates.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In this study, prospects of designing new Al–Ca–Cu–Mn (Zr) alloys for additive manufacturing (AM) were evaluated for the example of laser remelting of thin-sheet rolled products. The new as-cast alloys have a hypereutectic structure containing Al27Ca3Cu7 primary crystals and ultrafine eutectic particles of (Al,Cu)4Ca and Al27Ca3Cu7 phases in equilibrium with the aluminum solid solution. The solid solutions are additionally strengthened by alloying with Mn and micro additions of Zr, which contribute to the formation of coarsening-resistant phases without compromising the manufacturability of the alloys. Laser remelting, which simulates AM-typical solidification conditions, promotes the formation of a pseudoeutectic cellular structure without the occurrence of undesirable primary Al27Ca3Cu7. The size of the dendritic cells and eutectic particles is 10 times smaller (for solidification rates of ~200 K/s) than that of the as-cast state. This structure provides for a higher hardness of the laser-remelted alloy (96 HV) as compared to the as-cast alloy (85 HV). Data for the alloy after 350–400 °C long-term annealing for up to 100 h show that the hardness of the Al–Ca–Cu–Mn–Zr alloys declines relatively slowly by ~7.5% as compared to the Zr-free alloy, whose hardness decreases by ~22%. Thus, one can consider these alloys as a promising candidate for AM processes that require high thermal stability.</jats:p>

    4.2 High-temperature deformation mechanisms

Qualitatively, the creep behavior of the AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy follows the same trends as the

AM Al-Mg-Zr alloy previously studied by Griffiths et al., Fig. 3b [25]. That is, the as-fabricated

condition is most creep resistant and heat treatment, whether prior to creep testing or in-situ during

creep, reduces the creep resistance. Griffiths et al. attributed the reduced creep resistance to

coarsening of grain boundary particles, which led to increased grain boundary sliding. Given the

similar refined grain structure comprising of submicron equiaxed grains along MPBs and micron-

scale grains in the melt pool interior, grain boundary sliding is also the likely dominant high-

temperature deformation mechanism in the present AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy. Thus, a higher degree


                                                                            27of grain boundary coverage by θ-Al2Cu and other Cu-, Mn-, and Zr-rich precipitates is expected
to increase the high-temperature strength of AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr via inhibition of grain boundary

sliding. Several of the experimental observations support this theory. Note that in the context of

this discussion, we refer to grain boundary sliding which accommodates intragranular dislocation

movement, rather than grain boundary sliding which accommodates diffusional flow [48].


The KAM maps obtained post-creep, Fig. 7a–c, indicate that deformation is localized to grain

boundaries and the regions surrounding θ-Al2Cu particles, which are often at the grain boundaries.
Secondly, the degree of grain boundary coverage by particles correlates well with the observed

creep behavior. In the as-fabricated condition and after a 300 or 350 °C heat treatment prior to

creep, there is little distinguishable difference between the degree of grain boundary coverage by

θ-Al2Cu and other Cu-, Mn-, and Zr-rich precipitates after creep deformation, Figs. 8a–b. Each of
these heat treatments deform at a similar rate in the ~30–40 MPa stress range during creep.

However, the samples that were heat-treated at 400 °C prior to creep show clearly reduced levels

of grain boundary coverage after creep, with obvious PFZs surrounding the grain boundaries, Figs.

8c–d, and a substantial decrease in creep resistance relative to the other heat treatment conditions,

Fig. 3a. The divergence of the as-fabricated, 300 °C, 200 h, and 350 °C, 24 h creep curves at

stresses > ~40 MPa and strain rates > ~10-8 s-1 does not appear to be explainable in terms of grain

boundary sliding and the characterization performed in this study. However, there may be

additional contributing factors such as differing cavitation growth rates or direct deformation of

the grain interiors at higher stresses, which could lead to a divergence in the measured strain rates,

as recently observed in cast Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys with similar compositions to the present AM alloy

[43,49]. Compressive creep tests on this same alloy with the same heat treatment conditions, whose

results will be reported in a subsequent publication, will help explain the effects of tensile load on

the creep behavior.


Additionally, creep deformation dominated by grain boundary behavior rationalizes the apparent

lack  of L12-Al3Zr  strengthening  at  elevated  temperature,  Fig  2.  Since  high-temperature
deformation is localized to the grain boundaries and associated PFZs, the strength of the grain

interiors as determined by the size and number density of L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates is far less
important than at room temperature, where grain boundary sliding cannot occur. Dislocations may


                                                                            28also bypass the L12-Al3Zr by thermally activated climb at higher temperatures, which will further
decrease their strengthening potential. Experiments on alloys containing other types of L12
nanoprecipitates  e.g., Al3Sc and Al3Er, may be performed to elucidate the importance of
dislocation climb. These L12-precipitates have a higher lattice parameter mismatch with the Al
matrix and are therefore more efficient at arresting dislocations as they climb over [40,50].


The prevalence of grain boundary sliding does not preclude the load shuffling mechanism

postulated in Section 4.1. In fact, the two mechanisms likely act in concert. As the weakest areas

of the microstructure, the grain boundaries and associated PFZs both transfer load to the

precipitate-strengthened grain interiors and act as the primary deformation sites via grain boundary

sliding. As the grain boundary regions become weaker, the degree of load transfer to the grain

interiors is expected to increase. The interaction between the two mechanisms likely causes the
observed stress exponents 𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑝= 8–18 for dislocation creep to be higher than the expected value

of n = 2 for grain boundary sliding.


It is noted that the AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy (except for 400 °C, 200 h condition) despite its finer

grain size and lack of strengthening from the predominant secondary phase (θ particles located

mostly at grain boundaries), exhibits better creep resistance than its cast counterpart which is

strengthened by load-carrying submicron θʹ precipitates (Fig. 3b) [31]. This result underscores the

important role of minor secondary phases in AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy, including submicron θʹ-

Al2Cu, submicron Fe- Mn-, and Zr-rich particles, and nanoscale Al3Zr precipitates. These minor
phases strengthen the grain interior to the extent that deformation is mainly localized at the grain

boundaries, resulting in an improved creep resistance. The strengthening effect of the submicron

particles is supported by the observation of dislocation tangles around the particles in the crept

microstructures (Fig. 8) indicative of an Orowan-type strengthening mechanism.


    4.3 Future design strategies for creep-resistant AM Al alloys

Unsurprisingly, the refined grains in present AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy are deleterious to its creep

resistance and act as microstructural weak points prone to grain boundary sliding. However, even

with its refined grain structure, this AM alloy still exhibits improved creep resistance relative to

its cast counterpart in several aging conditions, Fig. 3b. Further improvement of AM alloys is

                                                                            29therefore warranted, and the results of this study highlight several relevant design considerations

for high-temperature strength.


Improved creep resistance will likely begin with strengthening of the grain boundaries. Since many

recent AM Al alloys have been designed for nucleation of refined and equiaxed grains as a means

of reducing hot tearing during the manufacturing process, this strategy will be applicable to several

different  alloy  classes [51–53].  In  this  context, we may  state  that  there  is an  inherent

microstructural conflict between hot tear resistance (increased grain boundary area desired) and

creep resistance (decreased grain boundary area desired) of AM aluminum alloys. Strengthening

of the grain boundaries may be achieved by a higher number density of particles on the grain

boundaries and/or smaller associated PFZs. This design strategy is similar to one recently outlined

for cast Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys, where additions of Ni, Co, and Sb modified the grain boundary

precipitate compositions, increased the amount of grain boundary coverage, and reduced the size

of associated PFZ areas, all of which contributed to increased creep resistance [54]. With increased

grain boundary strength, the load transfer to grain interiors will decrease and precipitates in the

grain interiors such as L12-Al3Zr may then be able to further enhance the high-temperature
strength. While the discussion here focuses on strengthening of grain boundaries, other researchers

have also demonstrated that strengthening of heterophase interfaces (e.g. L12 Al3Sc on Al/Al11Ce3
interfaces) can also enhance creep resistance [55].


A second and related consideration is the thermal stability and coarsening resistance of particles

at the grain boundaries. The primary grain boundary phase in the AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy is θ-

Al2Cu, which rapidly coarsens at the aging temperatures of this study, 300–400 °C [37]. If the
alloy composition and/or processing conditions were modified such that a more coarsening-

resistant grain boundary phase was present, such as one rich in Ce, Ni and Mn [15], the creep

strength may be maintained even after a heat treatment, resulting in an alloy with peak strength at

both ambient and elevated temperatures.

coarse eutectic regions are considered to follow the same solid-state transformation pathway.

did not impact the microstructure evolution during heat treatment. Therefore, the two regions

will be consolidated and identified as the eutectic solidification (ES) region. The eutectic

solidification region contained three phases: FCC Al, Al11Ce3, and Al20Mn2CeES. In the ES
region, the Al11Ce3 phase preferentially solidified near the boundary between eutectic colonies,

solidification front for complex thermal fields. Liquid advection in the melt pool driven by

Marangoni effects might generate fluctuations in the local temperature or composition. A second

possibility is that Al20Mn2Ce particles originate from partial remelting of powder particles or

info.name: update_plan

Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions

        - DEVICE: Device interventions

info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.

Abstract:
<jats:p>As a new alloy manufacturing method that can break through the limitations of molds to manufacture fine parts, laser powder bed fusion has recently become a common process for producing aluminum alloys. In the fields of aerospace or automotive, aluminum alloys with both good printability and good mechanical performance in high-temperature conditions are greatly demanded, and the Al-Ce alloy is one of the alloys with significant potential. Therefore, systematic research on the additive manufacturing of Al-Ce alloys is still being explored. Herein, we review the recent progress and current status of laser powder bed fusion-produced Al-Ce alloys, giving our opinions on the development of this alloy system. Element composition, alloy powders, laser powder bed fusion parameters, microstructures, and mechanical properties at room temperature and high temperatures are summarized. The choice of alloying strategies is crucial for a specific mechanical improvement of the Al-Ce alloys. Finally, the details of the Al-Ce alloys manufactured via laser powder bed fusion are presented.</jats:p>

## 5. Composites and Alloys Based on the Al-Ce System
Valid Text Names:

    publisher = "IntechOpen"
}


Abstract:
Aluminum alloys containing small amounts of cerium have been investigated to improve the grain refining, casting characteristics, and mechanical properties of aluminum alloys. These additions were usually made at levels of 1% or less but did not produce appreciable improvements. Recent work has shown that additions between 4% and the approximate eutectic composition of 10% improve the high-temperature performance of aluminum alloys. Corrosion performance of aluminum alloys can also be improved through the addition of Ce. Traditional aluminum alloying elements such as magnesium and silicon can be used to control casting characteristics and thermal and physical properties. Cerium oxide is the predominate oxide in rare earth mining. Much of it is discarded after separation from the heavy rare earth oxides containing Nd and Dy. The beneficial use of Ce should reduce the cost of the more desirable rare earths. Results of using Ce as an addition to aluminum in mul-tiple manufacturing methods such as additive manufacturing, extrusion, and casting are explored. The results show significant strengthening and improved mechanical property retention at higher temperatures than in other aluminum alloys and, in some compositions, show complete recovery of mechanical properties at room temperature when exposed to elevated temperatures as high as 500°C for 1000 hours.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Driven by the rapid advancement of key engineering domains such as aerospace, transportation, and marine systems, there is an urgent need for aluminum alloys exhibiting superior mechanical properties. Heterostructures, defined by inhomogeneous distributions of microstructural domains with distinct property gradients, have become a leading strategy to achieve a synergy between outstanding strength and satisfactory ductility. Additive manufacturing technologies, particularly laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), provide unparalleled design flexibility for creating heterogeneous microstructures. This review systematically classifies the various heterostructures in additively manufactured aluminum alloys, investigates the mechanisms enabling precise control of microstructural heterogeneity, and underscores the exceptional mechanical performance of L-PBF-processed alloys with such structures. Moreover, the challenges and opportunities associated with advancing heterostructured aluminum alloys via L-PBF are critically analyzed, highlighting the necessity for robust theoretical frameworks and scalable manufacturing approaches.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Inconel 718 (IN718) is a polycrystalline nickel-based superalloy and one of the most widely used materials in the aerospace industry owing to its excellent mechanical performances at high temperatures, including creep resistance. Interest in additively manufactured components in aerospace is greatly increasing due to their ability to reduce material consumption, to manufacture complex parts, and to produce out-of-equilibrium microstructures, which can be beneficial for mechanical behavior. IN718’s properties are, however, very sensitive to microstructural features, which strongly depend on the manufacturing process and subsequent heat treatments. Additive manufacturing and, more specifically, Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) induces very high thermal gradients and anisotropic features due to its inherently directional nature, which largely defines the microstructure of the alloy. Hence, defining appropriate manufacturing parameters and heat treatments is critical to obtain appropriate mechanical behavior. This review aims to present the main microstructural features of IN718 produced by LPBF, the creep mechanisms taking place, the optimal microstructure for creep strength, and the most efficient heat treatments to yield such an optimized microstructure.

Abstract:
The introduction of Sc/Zr inoculates to aluminium (Al) alloys for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) provides numerous benefits, including laser processability improvement, solidification microstructure control and mechanical property enhancement. Though great efforts have been put into tailoring the microstructure and room temperature mechanical properties via process parameter optimisations, the potential roles of Sc/Zr inoculate modified Al alloys for high-temperature applications were still underexplored. In this study, the microstructural stability and the elevated temperature tensile behaviours of LPBF-processed Al-Mn-Sc alloy were systematically evaluated. The alloy demonstrated high microstructural stability after both heat treatment and high-temperature tensile testing for up to 573 K. The applied tensile testing temperature and strain rate played significant influences on the elevated temperature tensile properties and deformation behaviours. Unusual intermediate temperature embrittlement (also known as ductility dip) and yield drop behaviours were observed under certain testing temperature and strain rate regimes, and the underlying deformation mechanisms were elucidated in detail. The present study is expected to shed light on future high-performance, high-temperature Al alloy development for the LPBF process.

Abstract:
Processing 7075 alloy by laser powder bed fusion is complex due to hot cracking. Zr addition is one of the solutions to reduce this susceptibility to cracking and permit the elaboration of crack-free parts. This study explored the microstructural and hardness evolutions of an Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-Zr alloy with respect to different heat treatment routes. In particular, natural and artificial agings are considered from as-built and solution heat-treated tempers. Microstructural characterization was principally carried out by optical, scanning, and transmission electron microscopy. In the as-built state, the melt pools exhibited a bimodal grain structure consisting of very fine grains at their boundaries and coarser elongated grains in the center. The grain boundaries were composed of η-Mg(Al, Zn, Cu)2 eutectic. The associated hardness is quite significant (140 HV0.1). Natural and artificial aging from this state did not show any significant microstructural and hardness evolutions. In contrast, solution heat treatments modified the microstructure by dissolving eutectics and Al3Zr precipitation without significant grain growth. Natural and artificial aging produced interesting hardening: a maximum of 220 HV0.1 was achieved for the T6 temper. The resulting value completely exceeded the hardness of the AW-7075-T6 alloy. This excellent value was attributed to η′ and Al3Zr precipitation without significant grain growth.

This study introduces a family of unique Al–Mn–Cr–Zr-based aluminium alloys illustrated by two ternary and one quaternary variants. The choice of alloy compositions has created a system resistant to solidification cracking while retaining high amount of solutes in solid solution in as-printed condition. Good relative density (~ 99.5%) has been demonstrated along with microstructural study supported by X-ray diffraction to display solidification structure with nanometric precipitate formation in small amounts in as-printed condition. High levels of Mn and Cr produce significant solid solution strengthening reaching hardness of up to 102 HV in as-printed condition. Additionally, the combination of Mn, Cr and Zr is shown to be important to control precipitation strengthening upon direct ageing and coarsening resistance due to slow diffusivity. Abstract:
The demand for high-performance aluminum components drives research into the design of novel alloys that can be processed by laser-based additive manufacturing. In recent years, the addition of grain refiners proved to be an effective strategy to reduce the hot-cracking of high-strength Al alloys. In this study, the solidification and aging behavior of an Al2139 alloy doped with additions of Zr and Ti for L-PBF was investigated. These elements favored the formation of a fine-grained structure free of cracks. The formation of Al3(Zr,Ti) inoculants was predicted by Scheil simulations and observed as cuboidal particles in the center of α-Al grains. The microstructure of the as-built material featured fine and fully equiaxed grains, which appeared comparatively finer at the edge (300–600 nm) and coarser (0.8–2.0 μm) at the center of the molten pools. In both cases, there was evidence of Cu and Mg micro-segregations at the grain boundaries. The microhardness of 109.7 HV0.5 in the as-built state was increased to 186.1 HV0.5 after optimized T4 heat treatment, responsible for the precipitation of many rod-shaped Zr- and Ti-based second phases and quasi-spherical Cu-, Mn-, and Fe-rich particles. Prolonged exposure carried out to simulate high-temperature service caused a drop in microhardness and marked modification of the microstructure, evidenced by the rearrangement and subsequent spheroidization of Cu- and Mg-rich particles at the grain boundaries.

This excerpt is directly relevant to Ekaputra’s scandium-free L-PBF Al-Zr-X alloys, but it reports only the study scope and headline findings, not the detailed creep-test matrix requested. The alloys are binary Al-0.4Zr and ternary Al-0.4Zr-1X (at.%), with X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W. Compressive creep was conducted at 400°C, and every ternary alloy had substantially better creep resistance than binary Al-Zr. The excerpt does not specify applied stresses, test durations, measured secondary creep rates, or rupture outcomes. For thermal aging, the relevant condition is 400°C; long-term exposure caused supersaturated ternary solutes to precipitate as binary Al-X phases. Mn and Cr precipitated faster than V, Mo, and W, while V, Mo, and W remained nearly entirely in solid solution after 2016 hours at 400°C. The excerpt states that ternary-solute strengthening at room temperature did not significantly differ among the five alloys or with aging time, implying a stable contribution despite precipitation, but it provides no numerical hardness values or detailed microstructural measurements. These alloys were tested in creep at 260 °C, including an 8-hour test and a 168-hour test. In the 8-hour test, as-fabricated material had an approximate threshold stress of 40 MPa, compared with approximately 14 MPa for material previously aged at 260 °C; thus, the as-fabricated condition was more creep-resistant. After 168 hours at 260 °C, the two conditions exhibited nearly identical creep behavior, attributed to coarsening of grain-boundary Al3Zr precipitates during testing. The excerpt does not report numerical minimum creep rates or stress-rupture failure. It also reports short-term yield results at 260 °C: 87 MPa for as-fabricated material versus 24 MPa for peak-aged material. Aging observations include peak aging at 400 °C for 8 hours, producing continuous approximately 2-nm and discontinuous approximately 5-nm Al3Zr precipitates; heating to 500 °C caused most precipitates and oxide particles to disappear. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufacturing (AM) can fabricate, repair, and join near-net-shaped components for high-performance engineering applications, including biomedical, energy, and transport sectors. The broader adoption of DED remains constrained by the limited number of alloys available that can be reliably manufactured without imperfections, hence limiting mechanical properties. Here, we designed an Al–Ni–Ce–Mn–Fe AM alloy that can achieve an ultra-fine microstructure (<5 μm), uniform distribution of intermetallics, low residual stress (<32 MPa), and superior mechanical properties in as-built DED components. Compared to DED AlSi10Mg in the as-built state using the same conditions, the yield increased by 70%, and the ultimate tensile strength by 50%. DED-AM involves rapid cooling and complex thermal conditions, which largely influence the property of the final components. Post-characterization cannot capture the time resolved thermal behavior, hence offer limited mechanism-based guide for alloy design. In this study, we develop a novel multimodal characterization methodology for correlative in situ X-ray imaging, X-ray diffraction, and infrared imaging, enabling quantification of the in situ thermal-related behavior, including phase evolution, temperature distribution, and stress accumulation during DED. We elucidated key mechanisms driving the structure refinement and stress development in this alloy. The insights gained into the interplay between alloy composition, thermal-related behavior, and performance under specific AM conditions inform next-generation material design tailored for AM technologies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a typical additive manufacturing technology that offers significant advantages in the production of complex components. With the rapid heating and cooling characteristics of LPBF, a large amount of solid solution of alloying elements in the matrix can be achieved to form supersaturated solid solutions, thus enhancing the properties of LPBF alloys. For the unique microstructure, the heat treatment process needs to be adjusted accordingly. In this work, a Zr/Sc-modified Al-Mg alloy processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with relatively low cost and good mechanical properties was investigated. The fine microstructure was obtained under rapid solidification conditions. The nanoscale Al3(Sc,Zr) particles precipitated at the molten pool boundary during solidification. These particles, as effective heterogeneous nucleators, further refined the α-Al grains and improved the mechanical properties of the alloy. As a result, the alloy exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure consisting of columnar grains in the center of the molten pool and equiaxed grains at the boundaries. The rapid solidification resulted in the supersaturation of solute atoms in the α-Al matrix, which significantly enhanced the solid solution strengthening effect. With the LPBF processing parameters of a combination of a laser power of 250 W, a laser scanning speed of 833 mm/s, and stripe scanning mode, the tensile strength of the alloy reached 401.4 ± 5.7 MPa, which was significantly higher than that of the cast alloys with aging treatment (281.1 ± 1.3 MPa). The heat treatment promoted the formation of secondary Al3(Sc,Zr), Mn/Mg-rich phases. The ultimate tensile strength and elongation at fracture after aging at 325 °C for 2 h were 536.0 ± 1.7 MPa and 14.8 ± 0.8%, respectively. The results provide insight into the preparation of aluminum alloys with relatively low cost and excellent mechanical properties.

Abstract:
Titanium and its alloys are widely employed in the aerospace industry, and their use will increase in the future. At present, titanium is mainly produced by the Kroll method, but this is expensive and energy-intensive. Therefore, the research of efficient and sustainable methods for its production has become relevant. The present review provides a description of the titanium recycling methods used to produce mostly aeronautical components by additive manufacturing, offering an overview of the actual state of the art in the field. More specifically, this paper illustrates that ilmenite is the main source of titanium and details different metallurgic processes for producing titanium and titanium alloys. The energy consumption required for each production step is also illustrated. An overview of additive manufacturing techniques is provided, along with an analysis of their relative challenges. The main focus of the review is on the current technologies employed for the recycling of swarf. Literature suggests that the most promising ways are the technologies based on severe plastic deformation, such as equal-channel angular pressing, solid-state field-assisted sintering technology-forge, and the Conform process. The latter is becoming established in the field and can replace the actual production of conventional titanium wire. Titanium-recycled powder for additive manufacturing is mainly produced using gas atomization techniques.

Abstract:
In this study, the effect of Zr elements on Al–10Ce alloys were investigated in terms of the microstructure, mechanical properties at room and high temperatures, and corrosion resistance. Meanwhile, the finite element simulations on tensile fracture was adopted to explain the fracture process of Al–Ce alloys. Results showed that as Zr content increased from 0.05 to 0.15%, the eutectic Al11Ce3 phase were gradually coarsened. However, further increase in Zr content led to the refinement and homogenization. Meanwhile, a significant transformation in the morphology of eutectic Al11Ce3 from layered to rod-like or bar-like structures happened. Correspondingly, mechanical properties at room temperature such as hardness, tensile strength, and yield strength initially decreased but subsequently increased. The tensile strength and yield strength of the alloys could reach the maximum values of 160 MPa and 96 MPa, respectively, and the elongation of the alloy reached the highest of 14.4%. The yield strength and the tensile strength at high temperature of 300 °C exhibited the highest values of 62.5 Mpa and 74 Mpa, respectively, when the Zr content is 0.05%. Moreover, the corrosion current of the alloys was minimized to 1.158 × 10− 7 µA/cm2 when the content of Zr was 0.05%, which attributed to the observed optimal microstructural characteristics of the Al11Ce3 phase at this concentration. Therefore, it is believed that Al–10Ce–Zr alloys are excellent candidate engineering materials in extreme environment fields.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Conventional precipitation‐strengthened aluminum alloys often lose load‐bearing capacity above approximately 300 °C as matrix softening accompanies precipitate coarsening or dissolution. Solidification‐derived intermetallic architectures offer an alternative route to elevated‐temperature strength through thermally stable lamellar, fibrous, cellular, divorced, or three‐dimensional networks. This review examines heat‐resistant aluminum alloys containing eutectic, near‐eutectic, primary‐phase‐plus‐eutectic, and rapidly solidified eutectic‐like architectures. A manufacturing‐process‐aware framework links alloy chemistry, local thermal history, intermetallic architecture, and defect population across casting, laser powder bed fusion, electron beam powder bed fusion, laser directed energy deposition, and wire arc additive manufacturing. Evidence is categorized into phase stability and hardness retention, instantaneous high‐temperature strength, creep and rupture, fatigue, and component‐scale qualification. Cross‐family comparisons show that refined spacing alone does not ensure heat resistance. Sustained performance also requires sufficient phase fraction, stable morphology and connectivity, matrix strength, interfacial integrity, and tolerance to route‐specific defects. Available studies demonstrate condition‐specific capability within parts of the 300–400 °C range, but the evidence remains uneven and often derives from unmatched test conditions. The resulting family–route–condition framework provides transferable reporting descriptors and qualification priorities without equating thermal stability with structural capability under sustained loading.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The capability for synergistic advancements in both making and shaping afforded by additive manufacturing (AM) enables the flexible production of high-performance components. Boosted by the growing demand for heat-resistant aluminum alloys in the moderate-temperature weight-critical applications, AM of heat-resistant aluminum alloys constitutes a burgeoning field. Although numerous advances have emerged in recent years, there remains a gap in the review literature elucidating the newly-developed alloy systems and critically evaluating the efficacy. This state-of-the-art review presents a detailed overview of recent achievements on the heat-resistant aluminum alloy development. It begins with the introduction of various AM technologies and the pros and cons of each technique are evaluated. The enhancement mechanisms associated with printability and high-temperature properties of AM aluminum alloys are then delineated. Thereafter, the various additively manufactured aluminum alloy systems are discussed with regard to the microstructure, heat resistance and high-temperature performance. An emphasis is put on the powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB) as it has garnered significant attention for heat-resistant aluminum alloys and the vast majority of the current studies are based on this technique. Finally, perspectives are outlined to provide guidance for future research.

Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Al-Ce and Al-Ce-Cr Cast Alloys: Effects of Cr and Solidification Conditions Valid Text Names: 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 1-6', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 6-11', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 11-15', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 15-22', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 22-27', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 27-32', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 32-35', 'junior2026microstructureandmechanical pages 35-36' BibTex: @article{junior2026microstructureandmechanical, author = "Júnior, Gueber Elias Mendes Santos and Oliveira, Leonardo Carvalho and Silva, Argos Soares and Leal, Jaderson Rodrigo Silva and Barros, André Santos and Xavier, Marcella Gautê Cavalcante and Spinelli, José Eduardo", title = "Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Al-Ce and Al-Ce-Cr Cast Alloys: Effects of Cr and Solidification Conditions", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Sep", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10918756/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10918756/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

Lightweight Al alloys capable of retaining mechanical performance at elevated temperatures are increasingly relevant for transportation and structural applications. Al-Ce alloys are particularly attractive because of their good castability and thermally stable Ce-containing intermetallics. However, how Cr addition modifies phase formation and mechanical behavior under rapid solidification remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the processing–microstructure–property relationships of Al–13Ce and Al–10Ce–1Cr (wt%) alloys produced by centrifugal solidification (CS), with directional solidification (DS) used for comparison. Abstract:
Iron-based high-temperature alloys are engineered to withstand extreme conditions, including elevated temperatures, mechanical stress, and corrosive environments. These alloys play a critical role in industries such as aerospace, power generation, and chemical processing, where materials must maintain structural integrity and performance under demanding operational conditions. This review examines recent advancements in iron-based alloys, with a focus on alloying strategies, high-temperature performance, and applications. Traditional approaches—including alloy design, microstructure control, process optimization, and computational modeling—continue to enhance alloy performance. Furthermore, emerging technologies such as high-entropy alloy (HEA) design, additive manufacturing (AM), nanostructured design with nanophase strengthening, and machine learning/artificial intelligence (ML/AI) are revolutionizing the development of iron-based superalloys, creating new opportunities for advanced material applications.
