               Coarsening- and creep behavior of supersaturated Al-Zr-X
         (X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, W) alloys processed by laser powder-bed fusion

     Clement N. Ekaputraa, Ekin Senvardarlia, Christian Leinenbachb,c, David C. Dunanda

         a Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208, USA

        b Empa, Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, Dübendorf 8600, Switzerland

                 c École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Laboratory for Photonic Materials and
                                   Characterization, Lausanne 1015, Switzerland


Abstract

We characterize the high-temperature microstructural evolution and creep properties of binary
Al-0.4Zr and ternary Al-0.4Zr-1X (at.%) alloys fabricated by laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF),
where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W are slow-diffusing transition metals added for solid-solution
strengthening. All alloys contain strengthening L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates which form during
aging at 400°C. In the as-fabricated alloys, the ternary solute is nearly all in solid solution in the
Mn- and Cr-containing alloys, and partially in solution in the V-, Mo-, and W-containing alloys,
but still in amounts well beyond the equilibrium solubility limit for these elements. Solid
solutions of the ternary solutes decompose during long-term aging at 400°C to form binary Al-X
precipitates. The relative rates of precipitation of these elements are consistent with their relative
diffusivities in Al: the precipitation rate is fastest for Mn, followed by Cr, then V, Mo, and W
(the latter three elements remain almost entirely in solid solution after 2016 h exposure at
400°C). Nevertheless, the strengthening contribution from the ternary solute at room temperature
does not significantly differ among the five studied alloys or as a function of aging time at
400°C, indicating a stable strengthening contribution from Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W in Al. During
creep deformation at 400°C, all ternary alloys show significantly higher creep resistance than a
binary Al-Zr alloy. Furthermore, their creep resistance is comparable to those of additively-
manufactured alloys with significantly higher volume fractions of strengthening phases.1. Introduction

Aluminum-based alloys processed by laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing
often have unique, non-equilibrium microstructures due to the fast cooling rates (>105-106 K/s)
inherent to the L-PBF process [1]. One important aspect of these non-equilibrium
microstructures is the ability to achieve extended solid solutions well beyond their maximum
equilibrium solubility [2]. As a result, Al-based alloys designed for additive manufacturing can
be more heavily alloyed than those designed for conventional, near-equilibrium solidification
(such as casting), and by extension often display much enhanced mechanical properties due to
greater solid-solution or secondary-precipitation strengthening [1].

One important example of such alloys are L12-strengthened Al alloys, where high amounts of
L12-forming elements (Sc, Zr, Ti) beyond their maximum solid solubilities in Al promote both
printability and large strengthening responses during secondary aging [3, 4]. Two prominent
commercial examples of such alloys are Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Scalmalloy) [5] and Al-Mg-Zr
(Addalloy) [6] alloys, but many similar alloys exist in the literature (e.g., Al-Mn-Mg-Sc-Zr [7],
Al-Mn-Cr-Zr [8], Al-Cu-Mn-Zr [9], Al-Cu-Sc-Zr [10], Al-Zn-Mg-Sc-Zr [11]), where high
amounts of additional alloying elements (Mg, Mn, Cu, Cr, Zn) beyond their equilibrium
solubility limits provide additional solid-solution or precipitation strengthening. In this work, we
focus on the high-temperature solid-solution strengthening effect of five transition metals in
ternary Al-Zr-X systems, for design of Al alloys with excellent high-temperature mechanical
properties.

Here, we study the addition of Mn, Cr, V, Mo, and W to the Al-Zr system. Among the various
solid-solution strengthening elements in Al, these five elements provide some of the highest
solid-solution strengthening increments per at.% added [1, 12]. This is due to their large lattice
misfit in Al: from first-principles calculations [12], a 75-125 MPa yield-strength increment can
be expected from 1 at.% addition of these elements, as opposed to <25 MPa/at.% from Mg or Zn.
However, the low equilibrium solid solubility of these elements in Al limits the amount that can
be added under conventional processes, but the rapid solidification rates provided by L-PBF AM
enables much higher amounts of these elements to be added in supersaturated solid solution,
increasing their possible solution strengthening effect. For example, Al-4.5Mn-1.3Mg-0.79Sc-
0.74Zr (wt.%) [13] and Al-5.0Mn-0.8Cr-0.6Zr (wt.%) [8] alloys processed by L-PBF fully retain
their respective amounts of Mn and Cr in solid solution after L-PBF, leading to high strength in
the as-fabricated state. Earlier work in the rapid solidification literature on the binary Al-Mn, Al-
Cr, Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-W systems [14] suggests that 2.2% Mn, 0.94% Cr, 0.53% V, 0.18%
Mo, and 0.18% W (at.%), respectively, is retained in solid solution for cooling rates of 103-104
K/s. Similar studies show as much as 2.0 at.% V [15], 2.45 at.% Mo [16], and 1.0 at.% W [17]
can be obtained for higher cooling rates (>105 K/s), which are more similar to the cooling rates
expected in L-PBF [1], suggesting high amounts of possible solid-solution strengthening from
alloys containing these elements.

Furthermore, previous experimental work indicates that slow-diffusing solute elements can also
provide resistance to creep deformation at high temperatures. The creep strengthening effect of
Mn solutes have been widely studied. In a study by Farkoosh et al. [18], the presence of just 0.5at.% Mn in an Al-0.5Mn-0.02Si alloy reduced creep strain rates at 300°C by 5-6 orders of
magnitude when compared to pure Al. In the same study, the dislocation creep threshold stress of
an Al-0.5Mn-0.09Zr-0.05Er-0.05Si alloy was more than three times higher than that of a similar
Al-0.11Zr-0.005Er (at.%) alloy without Mn. Similar results have been found in cast Al-Ce-Mn
[19] and L-PBF processed Al-Mn-Sc [20] alloys. In all these studies, it is proposed that attractive
forces exerted by slow-diffusing Mn atoms slow the climb of dislocations, reducing creep strain
rates. More generally, other slow-diffusing elements, such as Fe [21], also improve creep
resistance, while fast-diffusing elements such as Cu, Zn, and Bi [22] provide no creep
strengthening and may even increase creep strain rates.

A natural question, then, is whether solutes which diffuse even slower than Mn in Al – such as
Cr, V, Mo, and W – also have a stronger creep strengthening effect than Mn when in solid
solution in Al. The diffusivity of Mn at 400 °C is 9 x 10-19 m2/s, that of Cr is two orders of
magnitude lower (1.3 x 10-21 m2/s), and those of V, Mo, and W are 5-6 orders of magnitude
lower than Mn (5 x 10-24, 5 x 10-23, and 5 x 10-23 m2/s, respectively) [23]. Several previous
studies have examined the effects of slow diffusing elements (Cr, V, Mo, W) on the creep
resistance of Zr-containing cast Al alloys [24-28], but only in small amounts (<0.1 at.%) as the
achievable solubility of these elements in cast alloys is quite low. Earlier studies have reported
improved creep rupture life in more concentrated, rapidly-solidified, binary Al-Cr, -V, -Mo, or -
W alloys [14], but do not report the secondary creep strain rates in these alloys. Thus, there is a
gap in the literature on the creep properties of rapidly-solidified Al alloys strengthened by stable,
extended solid solutions.

Here, we study six L-PBF processed Al alloys: a binary Al-0.4Zr alloy, and five ternary Al-
0.4Zr-1X (at.%) alloys, where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W are all slow-diffusing transition metal
elements. The 1 at.% concentration of the ternary solute is selected based on the above literature
suggesting that this amount could be retained in solid solution for rapidly-solidified binary Al-X
alloys, and kept constant between alloys to isolate effects of the solute itself on microstructure
and mechanical properties. We focus first on the as-fabricated, rapidly-solidified microstructure
of these alloys to determine if supersaturated solid solutions of these elements can be achieved.
Then, we evaluate the stability of these solid solutions during aging at temperatures >400°C, and
the effect of any precipitation on the room-temperature microhardness. Lastly, we study the
effect of these alloying elements on compressive creep properties at 400°C, comparing the effect
of alloying element and aging condition.2. Experimental procedures

Six alloy compositions were prepared: a binary Al-0.4Zr (at.%) alloy, and five ternary Al-0.4Zr-
1X (at.%) alloys, where X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo, or W. For brevity, these alloys will be referred to as
Al-Zr and Al-Zr-X alloys. Bi

Abstract:
With development of present energy-saving society, lightweight and green development in the automotive and aerospace industries have put forward urgent demands for heat-resistant cast aluminum alloys. Present cast aluminum alloys are of lightweight and have excellent mechanical properties when serving in ambient environment. However, when serving at temperatures of 200–300 ℃ or even higher, the alloys inevitably soften and the high-temperature mechanical properties decline rapidly, hardly meeting the requirements for high-performance equipments. This paper summarizes the development process of classic heat-resistant aluminum alloys, especially the microstructural characteristics of heat-resistant cast aluminum alloys in the past decade, and reviews the current microstructure tuning strategies of heat-resistant aluminum alloys from the aspects of intrinsic heat resistance of the second phases, phase interface modification, diffusion-controlled phase transition, grain boundary stabilization and composite material design. Finally, we propose the prospects for the future development of heat-resistant aluminum alloys.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The samples of the Al–15Fe (mass%) binary alloy that were additively manufactured by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) were exposed to intermediate temperatures (300 and 500 °C), and the thermally induced variations in their microstructural characteristics were investigated. The L-PBF-manufactured sample was found to have a microstructure comprising a stable θ-Al13Fe4 phase localized around melt-pool boundaries and several spherical metastable Al6Fe-phase particles surrounded by a nanoscale α-Al/Al6Fe cellular structure in the melt pools. The morphology of the θ phase remained almost unchanged even after 1000 h of exposure at 300 °C. Moreover, the nanoscale α-Al/Al6Fe cellular structure dissolved in the α-Al matrix; this was followed by the growth (and nucleation) of the spherical Al6Fe-phase particles and the precipitation of the θ phase. Numerous equiaxed grains were formed in the α-Al matrix during the thermal exposure, which led to the formation of a relatively homogenous microstructure. The variations in these microstructural characteristics were more pronounced at the higher investigated temperature of 500 °C.</jats:p>

The excerpt provides the Sisco et al. 2023 findings for LPBF Al-Ce-Mn, but it does not state the alloy’s exact bulk Ce/Mn composition, nor does it report hardness or strength measurements. The specimen was heat treated isothermally at 400 °C for 1000 h. Relative to the as-fabricated condition, which contained FCC Al, Al20Mn2Ce, and Al11Ce3, heat treatment produced additional Al6Mn, Al12Mn, and Al51Mn7Ce4 phases. The refined heat-treated phase fractions were FCC Al (50.9 ± 0.04 wt.%), Al20Mn2Ce (1.4 ± 0.02 wt.%), Al11Ce3 (8.2 ± 0.01 wt.%), Al6Mn (17.3 ± 0.04 wt.%), Al12Mn (5.5 ± 0.04 wt.%), and Al51Mn7Ce4 (16.7 ± 0.03 wt.%). Thus, Al20Mn2Ce decomposed during exposure, with the text indicating that particles in the eutectic region followed the same pathway as those in the melt-pool-boundary region. Al11Ce3 was treated as stable because it is an equilibrium phase at 400 °C and was not expected to decompose. The excerpt contains no information about the requested comparative LPBF Al-15Fe Wang 2022 treatment at 300 °C for 1000 h, or the Al-Mn-Cr-Zr Mehta et al. 2023 treatment at 350 °C for 1000 h and associated hardness changes.

Richard A. Michi1, Sumit Bahl1, Christopher M. Fancher1, Kevin Sisco2, Lawrence F. Allard1,

Ke An3, Dunji Yu3, Ryan R. Dehoff4, Alex Plotkowski1, Amit Shyam1*


1Materials Science and Technology Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN

2Department of Mechanical, Aerospace, and Biomedical Engineering, University of Tennessee,

Knoxville, TN

3Neutron Scattering Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN

4Manufacturing Science Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN


*Corresponding author: A. Shyam (email: [email redacted]; phone: +18652414841)


Abstract

The high-temperature deformation behavior of an additively manufactured Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy is

evaluated in the as-fabricated and heat-treated states using traditional ex-situ and in-situ neutron

diffraction creep experiments performed at 300 °C. The dominant reinforcement phase in the alloy,

θ-Al2Cu, despite its high volume fraction of ~10%, does not provide load transfer strengthening
during creep deformation. Instead, the lattice strain evolution suggests a new mechanism we term

“load shuffling” wherein the initial load is transferred away from precipitate-free zones along the

grain boundaries where most of the θ-Al2Cu particles are located to precipitate-strengthened grain
interiors. Notwithstanding the lack of load transfer strengthening, the as-fabricated AM Al-Cu-

Mn-Zr alloy still possesses improved creep resistance at 300 °C relative to a cast alloy with similar

composition. The proposed load shuffling mechanism explains the lack of observed L12-Al3Zr
strengthening at 300 °C and helps identify several strategies for improvement of elevated-

temperature mechanical response of AM Al alloys.


Keywords: Additive manufacturing, neutron diffraction, creep, aluminum alloys, load transfer





                                                                             21.  Introduction

By utilizing the unique processing conditions associated with additive manufacturing (AM), it may

be possible to design novel high-temperature Al alloys for use in the 200–450 °C temperature

range, where traditional Al alloys lose their strength and consequently, heavier and/or more

expensive Ti alloys and steels are utilized [1]. As the range and scope of Al alloys which are

suitable for AM processing continues to grow [2–4], several recent studies have begun to realize

their potential for high-temperature performance.


Some examples of new Al alloys laser powder bed processed for elevated temperature applications

follow. Binary AM Al-Fe alloys with 2–15 wt.% Fe have been reported which are strengthened by

the nanometric metastable Al6Fe phase. These alloys maintain their strengths after hundreds of
hours aging at 300 °C, and the Al-15Fe alloy exhibits a compressive yield strength of 340 MPa at

300 °C [5–8]. In another binary alloy, AM Al-5.7Ni, a yield strength at 300 °C of 137 ± 2 MPa

was reported, which is 66 MPa higher than AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg at the same temperature [9,10].

Alloys containing several wt.% Ce which promotes formation of Ce-rich strengthening phases

upon solidification have also been developed, including Al-10Ce-8Mn [11], Al-9Cu-6Ce-(1Zr)

[12,13], Al-11Ce-7Mg and Al-15Ce-9Mg [14], Al-11Ce-3Ni-1Mn [15], and Al-8Ce-0.2Sc-0.1Zr

(laser-surface-remelted) [16]. The inherent coarsening resistance of the Ce-rich phases due to low

solubility and diffusivity of Ce in the Al matrix [17] contributes to the strength retention of these

alloys after hundreds of hours aging at 300–400 °C and, combined with microstructural refinement

from AM processing, contributes to elevated temperature yield strengths consistently superior to

those of AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg [9] and Scalmalloy®, two common alloys used for AM of Al.


Despite the lightweighting potential of these high-temperature alloys, creep deformation studies

which are critical for long-lifetime component design are not common. There have been a handful

of creep studies at 150–300 °C on the widely used AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg alloy [9,18–22]. During

creep deformation, the cellular eutectic Si network rapidly coarsens, which contributes to a

decrease in the creep resistance. However, the alloy does have comparable creep resistance at 300

°C to cast high-temperature alloys such as Al-10Ce-5Ni [23] and Al-7Ce-9Mg [24], suggesting

that despite its lack of microstructural coarsening resistance, AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg may still be an

acceptable candidate for use at ~300 °C. The 260 °C creep resistance of AM Al-10Si-0.3Mg is

                                                                             3similar to as-fabricated AM Al-2.9Mg-2.1Zr, which is strengthened by L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates
and Mg in solid solution [25]. However, the creep threshold stress of the AM Al-Mg-Zr alloy drops

dramatically from ~40 MPa in the as-fabricated state to ~14 MPa after either a peak aging

treatment at 400 °C or in-situ aging during creep at 260 °C [25]. The drop in creep strength was

attributed to grain boundary sliding enabled by the coarsening and subsequent reduced pinning

effectiveness of grain boundary particles and the prevalence of refined grains on the order of ~0.8

μm  in  diameter. A high volume  fraction (~35%)  of submicron and  coarsening-resistant

intermetallic phases contributed to the excellent creep resistance recently reported in a Al-11Ce-

3Ni-1Mn alloy at 300–400 °C [15]. This alloy has creep resistance at 300 °C approaching that of

advanced powder metallurgy Al alloys [26] and is a likely template for design of future creep-

resistant AM Al alloys.


Despite these existing creep studies, there is still a need for greater understanding of how common

microstructural features in AM Al alloys such as refined grains, dispersoids, precipitates and melt

pool boundaries affect the creep behavior. The present contribution deals with another common

microstructural feature of the high-temperature AM Al alloys mentioned thus far: a high volume

fraction (> ~10%) of reinforcing phase. This volume fraction of reinforcement is expected to result

in load transfer to the harder reinforcing particles from the softer Al matrix during creep

deformation [15,27–30]. Although load transfer has been inferred in many of the papers cited

herein, to our knowledge it has never been directly measured in an AM aluminum alloy. For a cast

Al-Cu alloy, it was recently revealed through in-situ neutron diffraction that a strengthening θ'-

Al2Cu phase shoulders a significant portion of the load during 300 °C creep deformation [31]
which was similar to the mechanical response of the same phase under ambient temperature

monotonic deformation [32]. Load transfer during creep of microstructurally similar Al metal

matrix composites has been directly measured in situ using neutron diffraction [33–35]. Results

from these studies indicate that the load transfer response is highly sensitive to reinforcement

volume fraction, coherency, crystallography, and morphology. For example, 0.5 μm diameter SiC

whiskers provide significantly higher load transfer compared to similar volume fractions of 20 μm

SiC particles [33].





                                                                             4In this study, we evaluate an AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy using conventional tensile creep tests and in-

situ neutron diffraction creep tests to explain the effects of load transfer on the high-temperature

performance of AM Al alloys. The results are linked to the alloy microstructure as evaluated on

multiple length scales across several different heat treatment conditions. Recent studies have

shown that the chosen AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy possesses a favorable combination of room

temperature yield strength (279 MPa) and ductility (11%) in the as-fabricated state [36,37]. The

alloy is heat-treatable, and the room-temperature yield strength can be further improved to 341

                                               I.    INTRODUCTION



      With the expansion of additive manufacturing (AM), there is a desire for materials

that are lightweight, low cost, and can be used in high temperature environments, such as

in engines or aerospace applications. Many high-temperature aluminum alloys face issues

during AM production such as solidification cracking [1,2,3] and high cost [3]. Al-Ce

alloys are being explored due to their outstanding printability [4], the relative low cost of

cerium [5], and thermal stability [6]. Al-10Ce (wt.%) is a near-eutectic binary alloy with a

narrow solidification range. To determine the feasibility of AM Al-Ce alloys in high

temperature applications, the creep property will be evaluated at homologous temperatures

between 0.6 and 0.75. By testing such a binary alloy, the effect of cerium on the mechanical

properties of AM aluminum alloy can be  isolated. The microstructure, mechanical

properties, and creep results will also be compared to cast Al-10Ce to explore the effect

AM has on the material.


      While aluminum alloys are lightweight, low cost, and corrosion resistant, their

microstructural stability and high temperature strength degrade rapidly with increasing

temperature and over time, limiting their high-temperature applications [3]. Currently, few

commercial high-temperature aluminum alloys are available [3]. One method of increasing

aluminum’s high temperature stability is through solid solution strengthening by alloying

with solutes such as Mg or Mn, or through precipitation strengthening by alloying with

rare earth elements such as Sc or Zr [3]. Sc and Zr have been used as alloying elements to

increase strength through precipitation and prevent intermetallic coarsening during aging

[6]. Cerium has been shown to have a similar effect on the temperature stability [7] at a                                                                       2


lower cost, between 80-100 times less expensive than other rare earth elements [5,8]. Die

cast eutectic Al-Ce alloy has a σ0.2 = 50 MPa and a UTS = 152 MPa [9], maintaining 80%

of its room-temperature mechanical properties at 240 °C. The intermetallic phase (Al11Ce3)

precipitates dendritically in a “Chinese script” morphology and provides strengthening [7].

Although Ce has been shown to improve thermal stability of Al alloys, it remains unknown

what effect it may have on the mechanical properties of AM Al alloys, given their refined

grain structure [10] and increased dislocation density [11].


      Cerium lends thermal stability to aluminum as an alloying element by nature of its

interaction with the fcc α-Al matrix. Al11Ce3 forms at the eutectic temperature of 644.5°C

and is arranged geometrically within the α-Al matrix [12]. The Al11Ce3 phase acts as

reinforcement, with a hardness of 350 HV compared to the aluminum matrix at 35 HV

[12]. However, alloying with cerium alone improves the strength of the alloy very little.

The benefit of cerium comes from the low diffusivity and solubility of cerium in aluminum.

Cerium has a diffusion coefficient about 4 orders of magnitude lower than Mg, Si, Zn, or

Cu [13, 14, 15]. The solid-state solubility of cerium in aluminum is near-zero, reaching an

estimated maximum of 0.01 wt.% at the eutectic temperature [8].


      The uncertainty of the effect of localized heating and repeated melting and

solidification in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) on the behavior of metallic alloys limits

the materials currently available for AM [4]. Primarily, only AlSi10Mg is certified for

metal AM as other commercial Al alloys are prone to solidification cracking [1,2].

However, the mechanical properties of near-eutectic Al-Si compositions cannot compete

with 2xxx or 7xxx series aluminum alloys [16]. While AlSi10Mg produced by LPBF shows

improved creep resistance compared to  its  traditionally cast counterpart, the  stress

4.1. Solute supersaturation in L-PBF Al-Zr-X alloys

Supersaturated solid solutions of Zr and the ternary alloying element X (Cr, V, Mo, and W) were
observed in both the binary Al-Zr and ternary Al-Zr-X alloys. These solid solutions were
observed directly via APT analyses (Fig. 5), and indirectly via SEM (Fig. 4) and electrical
conductivity analyses (Fig. 8). These supersaturated solid solutions are achieved in the L-PBF
Al-Zr-Cr, -V, -Mo, and -W alloys in concentrations beyond what was attainable in the arc-melted
alloys, due to the faster solidification rates in L-PBF..

The Al-Zr-Mn and -Cr alloys did not show obvious primary precipitates, unlike the Al-Zr-V, -
Mo, and -W alloys, which is attributed to the varying solidification intervals of these alloys. In
the Al-Zr-Mn alloy, a supersaturated solid solution was achieved in both the arc-melted and L-
PBF processed alloys. In the binary Al-Mn system, the solidification interval is quite small (1°C
for 1 at.% Mn, calculated via Thermo-Calc, TCAL8 database), and as a result little undercooling
is required to trap Mn in solution. This is consistent with the high amounts of Mn in solid
solution observed in the arc-melted Al-Zr-Mn alloy, as well as in other studies where as much as
~2 at.% Mn was retained in solution. For Al-Cr, the solidification interval is much larger (101°C
for 1 at.% Cr), which is qualitatively consistent with little solute supersaturation in the arc-
melted alloy, but much greater amounts in the L-PBF processed alloy. For Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-
W, the solidification intervals are even larger (315, 205, and 375°C for 1 at.% V, Mo, W
respectively). In the L-PBF process, it is well-established that the solidification velocity and
cooling rates are lowest at the meltpool boundary, and fastest at the center of the meltpool [6].
As a result, the slower cooling rates at the meltpool boundaries are insufficient to fully suppress
primary Al-X precipitation in the V-, Mo-, and W-containing alloys, but the faster cooling rates
near the center of the meltpool are sufficient, as observed for primary Al3Zr precipitates in many
other Al-Zr based alloys [6, 7, 46].

These observations are consistent with previous results in the rapid solidification and L-PBF
literature. Fedorov and Elagin [14] studied supersaturation in binary Al-X alloys (the same
elements as studied here), where mm-size granules were cooled from the melt at a rate of 103-104
K/s. In their study, the maximum achievable solute supersaturation in various binary Al-X alloys
was 2.2% Mn, 0.94% Cr, 0.53% V, 0.18% Mo, and 0.18% W (at.%). For our Al-Zr-Mn and Al-
Zr-Cr alloys, the high supersaturation of Mn and Cr is consistent with the extended solubility for
these elements observed by the above authors [14] at 103-104 K/s. Other researchers have
studied rapid solidification of these binary Al-Mn [47] and Al-Cr [48-50] systems, and observed
even greater extended solutions (up to 5 wt.%) for both Mn and Cr. Mn and Cr have also been
studied in L-PBF processed alloys [8, 13, 51] and extended solid solutions of up to 4.5 wt.% Mn
and 3 wt.% Cr have been observed in L-PBF. In rapidly solidified Al-V, Al-Mo, and Al-W alloys
cooled at a rate of 105-106 K/s (similar to L-PBF), as much as 2 at.% V [15], 1.3 at.% Mo [16],
and 1.0 at.% W [17], which is consistent with the microstructures of the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W
alloys at the center of the meltpool. However, the cooling rates at the meltpool boundary may be
insufficient to trap the amounts of V, Mo, and W added to these Al-Zr-X alloys. In Al-Mn-Sc
alloys with similar microstructure, the presence of primary Mn-rich intermetallic precipitatesnear the meltpool boundary can initiate failure there [52]. In these Al-Zr-X based alloys, it may
therefore be desirable to lower the ternary solute content for similar reasons, but more studies are
required to quantify the effect of solute content on mechanical properties.


4.2. Stability of supersaturated solid solutions with ternary solute

The supersaturated solid solutions of the Al-Zr-X alloys decompose during aging to form binary
Al-X precipitates, but at varying rates as evidenced by microstructural and electrical conductivity
investigations. From electrical conductivity studies (Fig. 8), sharp increases in conductivity
during aging at 400°C occurred after ~1 day in the Al-Zr-Mn alloy, after ~1 month in the Al-Zr-
Cr alloy, but were not observed in the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, or -W alloys after the longest time studied
here (2016 h or ~3 months). In the latter three alloys, the conductivity increases during aging at
a higher temperature (590°C) for 24h. These conductivity results are consistent with
microstructural studies (via SEM in Fig. 9, XRD in Fig. S4), which clearly show intragranular
precipitates in the Al-Zr-Mn alloy after 400°C/8h aging, in the Al-Zr-Cr alloy after 400°C/1008h
aging, and in the Al-Zr-V, -Mo, and -W alloys only after 590°C/24h aging.

The relative rates of precipitation align with the diffusivities of the ternary solute elements at

precipitation was observed to initiate after 6h at 500°C. While the aging procedures used in these
two studies [47, 49] are somewhat different, the higher initiation temperature for precipitation in

5. Conclusions

Advancement to the pre-established Al-Mn-Cr-Zr family of alloys tailored for PBF-LB process has
been shown. The new variants with increased Zr content and addition of Mg showed high as-
printed hardness of 132 HV in the most alloyed version (alloy F). Addition of Mg alone caused
solidiﬁcation cracking (alloy E) and was balanced by increasing Zr content (alloy F). As a result,
heavy grain reﬁnement with bimodal grain distribution is caused leading to tentative isotropic
properties. Direct ageing response reveal faster precipitation kinetics than previously established
in alloy C. The amount of hardening via direct ageing in alloy F was similar to alloy C (40 HV)
making the peak hardness reach 172 HV after ageing 623 K 24 h and 648 K 8 h, which suggests

Our hypothesis is that controlling the nucleation barrier for certain phases within the

The current research was motivated by these unexplained spatially varying phase transformations

observed in AM Al-Ce-Mn. The AM Al-10Ce-8Mn (wt. %) [Al-2.2Ce-4.5Mn (at. %)] alloy was

used because of the variety of solidification conditions across an individual weld track produced

a range of microstructures in a single sample. Our research focuses on characterization of the

phase evolution as a function of initial microstructural features, and then compares the results

with other processing routes in the literature. The overarching goals are as following: (1)

understand the range of initial metastable conditions in the AM microstructure; (2) classify the

subsequent solid-state phase transformations within the system, and validate our hypothesis that

the phase transformation pathways are the result of nucleation barriers for a third phase at the

interface of two parent phases created by AM.

An Al-10Ce-8Mn (wt.%) [or Al-2.2Ce-4.5Mn (at. %)], alloy was produced by melting and

mixing of raw materials in a 250 kg SiC crucible using an argon cover gas. Cast ingots were

distribution. AM was performed using a Concept Laser M2 laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF)

system. A more detailed description of the alloy production and composition is found by

Plotkowski et al [26]. There is notably slight Si contamination in the alloy as measured by

Abstract:
Diesel engines in heavy-duty vehicles are predicted to maintain a stable presence in the future due to the difficulty of electrifying heavy trucks, mine equipment, and railway cars. This trend encourages the effort to develop new aluminum alloy systems with improved performance at diesel engine conditions of elevated temperature and stress combinations to reduce vehicle weight and, consequently, CO2 emissions. Aluminum alloys need to provide adequate creep resistance at ~300 °C and room-temperature tensile properties better than the current commercial aluminum alloys used for powertrain applications. The studies for improving creep resistance for aluminum casting alloys indicate that their high-temperature stability depends on the formation of high-density uniform dispersoids with low solid solubility and low diffusivity in aluminum. This review summarizes three generations of diesel engine aluminum alloys and focuses on recent work on the third-generation dispersoid-strengthened alloys. Additionally, new trends in developing creep resistance through the development of alloy systems other than Al-Si-based alloys, the optimization of manufacturing processes, and the use of thermal barrier coatings and composites are discussed. New progress on concepts regarding the thermal stability of rapidly solidified and nano-structured alloys and on creep-resistant alloy design via machine learning-based algorithms is also presented.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study employs a combined approach of theoretical calculations and experimental validation to systematically optimize the alloy composition, aiming to mitigate the hot cracking susceptibility of an Al-3.0Ce-xCa-yMn alloy in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processing. Through advanced characterization techniques such as electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and mechanical property testing, the intrinsic relationship between microstructure and mechanical performance was thoroughly elucidated. Computational results revealed that the addition of Ca significantly lowered the eutectic precipitation temperature, thereby effectively reducing the hot cracking tendency while maintaining a stable volume fraction of the Al11(Ce, Ca)3 phase. The optimal mass fractions of calcium (Ca) and manganese (Mn) were determined to be 0.8% and 1.9%, respectively. Microstructural characterization indicates that the alloy consisted of an α-Al matrix embedded with Al-Ce-Ca ternary eutectic compounds, and nanoscale Al6Mn spherical precipitates were uniformly distributed within the matrix. Mechanical property evaluations demonstrated that the Al-3Ce-0.8Ca-1.9Mn alloy exhibited an outstanding balance of strength and ductility at both room and elevated temperatures, with room temperature yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation values of 321 ± 15 MPa, 429 ± 8 MPa, and 10.9 ± 2.3%, respectively. This exceptional performance was attributed to a synergistic combination of multiple strengthening mechanisms including eutectic structure-induced strengthening, grain boundary strengthening due to ultrafine grains, and dislocation pinning strengthening caused by nano-sized Al6Mn precipitates.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In this study, prospects of designing new Al–Ca–Cu–Mn (Zr) alloys for additive manufacturing (AM) were evaluated for the example of laser remelting of thin-sheet rolled products. The new as-cast alloys have a hypereutectic structure containing Al27Ca3Cu7 primary crystals and ultrafine eutectic particles of (Al,Cu)4Ca and Al27Ca3Cu7 phases in equilibrium with the aluminum solid solution. The solid solutions are additionally strengthened by alloying with Mn and micro additions of Zr, which contribute to the formation of coarsening-resistant phases without compromising the manufacturability of the alloys. Laser remelting, which simulates AM-typical solidification conditions, promotes the formation of a pseudoeutectic cellular structure without the occurrence of undesirable primary Al27Ca3Cu7. The size of the dendritic cells and eutectic particles is 10 times smaller (for solidification rates of ~200 K/s) than that of the as-cast state. This structure provides for a higher hardness of the laser-remelted alloy (96 HV) as compared to the as-cast alloy (85 HV). Data for the alloy after 350–400 °C long-term annealing for up to 100 h show that the hardness of the Al–Ca–Cu–Mn–Zr alloys declines relatively slowly by ~7.5% as compared to the Zr-free alloy, whose hardness decreases by ~22%. Thus, one can consider these alloys as a promising candidate for AM processes that require high thermal stability.</jats:p>

    4.2 High-temperature deformation mechanisms

Qualitatively, the creep behavior of the AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy follows the same trends as the

AM Al-Mg-Zr alloy previously studied by Griffiths et al., Fig. 3b [25]. That is, the as-fabricated

condition is most creep resistant and heat treatment, whether prior to creep testing or in-situ during

creep, reduces the creep resistance. Griffiths et al. attributed the reduced creep resistance to

coarsening of grain boundary particles, which led to increased grain boundary sliding. Given the

similar refined grain structure comprising of submicron equiaxed grains along MPBs and micron-

scale grains in the melt pool interior, grain boundary sliding is also the likely dominant high-

temperature deformation mechanism in the present AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy. Thus, a higher degree


                                                                            27of grain boundary coverage by θ-Al2Cu and other Cu-, Mn-, and Zr-rich precipitates is expected
to increase the high-temperature strength of AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr via inhibition of grain boundary

sliding. Several of the experimental observations support this theory. Note that in the context of

this discussion, we refer to grain boundary sliding which accommodates intragranular dislocation

movement, rather than grain boundary sliding which accommodates diffusional flow [48].


The KAM maps obtained post-creep, Fig. 7a–c, indicate that deformation is localized to grain

boundaries and the regions surrounding θ-Al2Cu particles, which are often at the grain boundaries.
Secondly, the degree of grain boundary coverage by particles correlates well with the observed

creep behavior. In the as-fabricated condition and after a 300 or 350 °C heat treatment prior to

creep, there is little distinguishable difference between the degree of grain boundary coverage by

θ-Al2Cu and other Cu-, Mn-, and Zr-rich precipitates after creep deformation, Figs. 8a–b. Each of
these heat treatments deform at a similar rate in the ~30–40 MPa stress range during creep.

However, the samples that were heat-treated at 400 °C prior to creep show clearly reduced levels

of grain boundary coverage after creep, with obvious PFZs surrounding the grain boundaries, Figs.

8c–d, and a substantial decrease in creep resistance relative to the other heat treatment conditions,

Fig. 3a. The divergence of the as-fabricated, 300 °C, 200 h, and 350 °C, 24 h creep curves at

stresses > ~40 MPa and strain rates > ~10-8 s-1 does not appear to be explainable in terms of grain

boundary sliding and the characterization performed in this study. However, there may be

additional contributing factors such as differing cavitation growth rates or direct deformation of

the grain interiors at higher stresses, which could lead to a divergence in the measured strain rates,

as recently observed in cast Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys with similar compositions to the present AM alloy

[43,49]. Compressive creep tests on this same alloy with the same heat treatment conditions, whose

results will be reported in a subsequent publication, will help explain the effects of tensile load on

the creep behavior.


Additionally, creep deformation dominated by grain boundary behavior rationalizes the apparent

lack  of L12-Al3Zr  strengthening  at  elevated  temperature,  Fig  2.  Since  high-temperature
deformation is localized to the grain boundaries and associated PFZs, the strength of the grain

interiors as determined by the size and number density of L12-Al3Zr nanoprecipitates is far less
important than at room temperature, where grain boundary sliding cannot occur. Dislocations may


                                                                            28also bypass the L12-Al3Zr by thermally activated climb at higher temperatures, which will further
decrease their strengthening potential. Experiments on alloys containing other types of L12
nanoprecipitates  e.g., Al3Sc and Al3Er, may be performed to elucidate the importance of
dislocation climb. These L12-precipitates have a higher lattice parameter mismatch with the Al
matrix and are therefore more efficient at arresting dislocations as they climb over [40,50].


The prevalence of grain boundary sliding does not preclude the load shuffling mechanism

postulated in Section 4.1. In fact, the two mechanisms likely act in concert. As the weakest areas

of the microstructure, the grain boundaries and associated PFZs both transfer load to the

precipitate-strengthened grain interiors and act as the primary deformation sites via grain boundary

sliding. As the grain boundary regions become weaker, the degree of load transfer to the grain

interiors is expected to increase. The interaction between the two mechanisms likely causes the
observed stress exponents 𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑝= 8–18 for dislocation creep to be higher than the expected value

of n = 2 for grain boundary sliding.


It is noted that the AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy (except for 400 °C, 200 h condition) despite its finer

grain size and lack of strengthening from the predominant secondary phase (θ particles located

mostly at grain boundaries), exhibits better creep resistance than its cast counterpart which is

strengthened by load-carrying submicron θʹ precipitates (Fig. 3b) [31]. This result underscores the

important role of minor secondary phases in AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy, including submicron θʹ-

Al2Cu, submicron Fe- Mn-, and Zr-rich particles, and nanoscale Al3Zr precipitates. These minor
phases strengthen the grain interior to the extent that deformation is mainly localized at the grain

boundaries, resulting in an improved creep resistance. The strengthening effect of the submicron

particles is supported by the observation of dislocation tangles around the particles in the crept

microstructures (Fig. 8) indicative of an Orowan-type strengthening mechanism.


    4.3 Future design strategies for creep-resistant AM Al alloys

Unsurprisingly, the refined grains in present AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy are deleterious to its creep

resistance and act as microstructural weak points prone to grain boundary sliding. However, even

with its refined grain structure, this AM alloy still exhibits improved creep resistance relative to

its cast counterpart in several aging conditions, Fig. 3b. Further improvement of AM alloys is

                                                                            29therefore warranted, and the results of this study highlight several relevant design considerations

for high-temperature strength.


Improved creep resistance will likely begin with strengthening of the grain boundaries. Since many

recent AM Al alloys have been designed for nucleation of refined and equiaxed grains as a means

of reducing hot tearing during the manufacturing process, this strategy will be applicable to several

different  alloy  classes [51–53].  In  this  context, we may  state  that  there  is an  inherent

microstructural conflict between hot tear resistance (increased grain boundary area desired) and

creep resistance (decreased grain boundary area desired) of AM aluminum alloys. Strengthening

of the grain boundaries may be achieved by a higher number density of particles on the grain

boundaries and/or smaller associated PFZs. This design strategy is similar to one recently outlined

for cast Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys, where additions of Ni, Co, and Sb modified the grain boundary

precipitate compositions, increased the amount of grain boundary coverage, and reduced the size

of associated PFZ areas, all of which contributed to increased creep resistance [54]. With increased

grain boundary strength, the load transfer to grain interiors will decrease and precipitates in the

grain interiors such as L12-Al3Zr may then be able to further enhance the high-temperature
strength. While the discussion here focuses on strengthening of grain boundaries, other researchers

have also demonstrated that strengthening of heterophase interfaces (e.g. L12 Al3Sc on Al/Al11Ce3
interfaces) can also enhance creep resistance [55].


A second and related consideration is the thermal stability and coarsening resistance of particles

at the grain boundaries. The primary grain boundary phase in the AM Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloy is θ-

Al2Cu, which rapidly coarsens at the aging temperatures of this study, 300–400 °C [37]. If the
alloy composition and/or processing conditions were modified such that a more coarsening-

resistant grain boundary phase was present, such as one rich in Ce, Ni and Mn [15], the creep

strength may be maintained even after a heat treatment, resulting in an alloy with peak strength at

both ambient and elevated temperatures.

{"answer": "**Yes.** Published studies report both creep or stress-rupture tests at ≥250 °C and *separate, unstressed* thermal exposures lasting ≥1000 h for scandium-free, laser-powder-bed-fused (LPBF) aluminum alloys. The distinction matters: a 1000 h aging result does not demonstrate 1000 h creep life. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000061)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

The clearest **stress-rupture measurements** include LPBF Al–10Ce: in Stinehart’s 2023 study, tensile specimens ruptured at 325 °C/21 MPa after 92.17 h, at 350 °C/21 MPa after 18.17 h, and at 350 °C/29 MPa after 6.1 h. Specimens tested at 300 °C/21 MPa and 300 °C/29 MPa were stopped *without rupture* after more than 765 and 546 h, respectively. The same work also measured compressive creep over 275–400 °C. A different, Sc-free LPBF Al–7.44Si–2.34Fe–1.79Mn–1.12Ni alloy was reported to last approximately 330 h in tensile creep at 400 °C/25 MPa. None of these results establishes a ≥1000 h rupture life. (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000059)

For the alloy families named in the question, **Al–Cu–Mn–Zr has direct creep data**: Michi and colleagues tested LPBF Al–8.6Cu–0.5Mn–0.9Zr at 300 °C. The stress associated with a minimum creep rate of 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹ was 56 MPa as fabricated, versus 30 MPa after a 400 °C/200 h pretreatment; this is evidence of creep measurement, not of 1000 h thermal stability. Griffiths and colleagues measured compressive creep of two Sc-free LPBF Al–Mg–Zr alloys at 260 °C, including an approximately 168 h test. Ekaputra and colleagues measured compressive creep of LPBF Al–0.4Zr–1X (at.%; X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo or W) at 400 °C; all five ternary compositions outperformed their binary Al–Zr comparator. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000035)

The **≥1000 h thermal-stability evidence** is also direct, but its conclusions differ by alloy. LPBF Al–10Ce–8Mn underwent 400 °C/1000 h exposure: the investigators observed decomposition of Al₂₀Mn₂Ce and formation of Al₆Mn, Al₁₂Mn and Al₅₁Mn₇Ce₄; this is measured phase evolution, *not* proof that the initial microstructure remained unchanged. For LPBF Al–5Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr (‘alloy C’), hardness fell by approximately 17–18 HV, or 13%, over 350 °C/1000 h; a related study characterized precipitates after 1078 h total at 350 °C. The suggestion that a different, Mg-containing variant would retain 140–150 HV after 1000 h was an **estimate**, not that variant’s measured result. (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000062)

Two further long exposures broaden the evidence. LPBF Al–15Fe was examined after 300 °C/1000 h: hardness decreased moderately, the initial nanoscale Al/Al₆Fe cellular structure changed, and stable Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitated; the study’s hardness-versus-time figure includes the 1000 h measurement. In LPBF Al–0.4Zr–1X, exposure extended to **2016 h at 400 °C**: Mn and Cr showed precipitation, whereas V, Mo and W remained almost entirely in solution; the authors reported broadly stable room-temperature strengthening contributions from the ternary solutes. These are observations of *unstressed* specimens and should not be reported as creep lives. (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000035)

**Bottom line:** the answer is unambiguously yes, including for Al–Ce, Al–Mn–Cr–Zr, Al–Cu–Mn–Zr and Al–Zr–Mn systems. What is substantially less established by the verified examples is **stress-rupture survival for ≥1000 h** at these temperatures: the cited ≥1000 h results are thermal-aging or microstructural measurements, while the specific rupture tests above ended sooner or were stopped before rupture. (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000019)"}

state.question: Has anyone measured creep, stress-rupture or long-exposure (1000 h or more) thermal stability at 250 C or above for a laser powder bed fusion aluminum alloy that contains no scandium, such as Al-Ce, Al-Fe-Zr, Al-Ni-Zr, Al-Mn-Zr or Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys?

answer.question: Has anyone measured creep, stress-rupture or long-exposure (1000 h or more) thermal stability at 250 C or above for a laser powder bed fusion aluminum alloy that contains no scandium, such as Al-Ce, Al-Fe-Zr, Al-Ni-Zr, Al-Mn-Zr or Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys?
answer.answer:
Yes. **Yes.** Published studies report both creep or stress-rupture tests at ≥250 °C and *separate, unstressed* thermal exposures lasting ≥1000 h for scandium-free, laser-powder-bed-fused (LPBF) aluminum alloys. The distinction matters: a 1000 h aging result does not demonstrate 1000 h creep life. (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 1-2, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 7-9, sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 5-8, stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 39-47)

| Alloy / primary report | Eligible exposure or test | Verified finding | Category |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary Al–10Ce (wt.%), Stinehart et al. (2023) | Tensile creep/stress rupture at 300–350 °C: 300 °C/21 MPa ran **>765 h without rupture**; 325 °C/21 MPa ruptured at 92.17 h; 350 °C/21 MPa at 18.17 h; 350 °C/29 MPa at 6.1 h | Direct rupture-life measurements; the >765 h result is right-censored and **not** evidence of a ≥1000 h creep test | Creep and stress rupture ≥250 °C (stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 39-47) |
| Al–3.6Mg–1.2Zr and Al–2.9Mg–2.1Zr (wt.%), Griffiths et al. (2020) | Compressive creep at 260 °C for 8 and 168 h | Approximate threshold stress was 40 MPa as fabricated versus 14 MPa after prior aging in the 8 h test; behavior converged after 168 h because grain-boundary Al₃Zr coarsened during testing | Creep ≥250 °C; no ≥1000 h exposure reported (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 1-2) |
| Al–8.6Cu–0.5Mn–0.9Zr (wt.%), Michi et al. (2023) | Tensile creep at 300 °C in as-fabricated and heat-treated conditions | Stress producing a minimum creep rate of 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹ fell from 56 MPa as fabricated to 30 MPa after 400 °C/200 h aging; heat treatment promoted precipitate-free zones and grain-boundary sliding | Creep ≥250 °C; aging was only 200 h (michi2023loadshufflingduring pages 30-33, michi2023loadshufflingduring pages 27-30) |
| Al–0.4Zr–1X (at.%), X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo or W, Ekaputra et al. (2026) | Compressive creep at 400 °C; separate **unstressed** aging at 400 °C for as long as 2016 h | Every ternary alloy was substantially more creep resistant than binary Al–0.4Zr. Mn and Cr precipitated during aging, whereas V, Mo and W remained almost entirely in solution after 2016 h; their room-temperature strengthening contribution remained broadly stable | Creep ≥250 °C **and** unstressed aging ≥1000 h (ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 1-4, ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 21-25) |
| Al–10Ce–8Mn (wt.%), Sisco et al. (2023) | **Unstressed** LPBF specimens aged at 400 °C for 1000 h | Metastable Al₂₀Mn₂Ce decomposed; Al₆Mn, Al₁₂Mn and Al₅₁Mn₇Ce₄ formed, while equilibrium Al₁₁Ce₃ remained. This report did not measure creep | Unstressed thermal stability ≥1000 h only (sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 5-8, sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 13-18) |
| Al–5.0Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr (wt.%, Alloy C), Mehta et al. (2023–2024) | **Unstressed** aging at 350 °C for 1000 h; separate detailed characterization after 24 h peak aging plus 1054 h, or 1078 h total | Hardness began declining after about 200 h and lost only 17–18 HV (about 13%) by 1000 h. At 1078 h total, precipitates occupied about 18 area% and included Cr-bearing Al₁₂Mn and Al₆Mn | Unstressed thermal stability ≥1000 h; no creep reported (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 7-9, mehta2024roleofcr pages 3-4) |
| Al–15Fe (wt.%), Wang et al. (2022) | **Unstressed** exposure at 300 °C for 1000 h | Hardness decreased moderately from approximately 200 HV. The nanoscale α-Al/Al₆Fe cellular structure largely dissolved, spherical metastable Al₆Fe particles grew, and stable plate-shaped θ-Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitated | Unstressed thermal stability ≥1000 h only (wang2022microstructuralvariationsin pages 5-8, wang2022microstructuralvariationsin media a4102c0d) |
| Al–7.44Si–2.34Fe–1.79Mn–1.12Ni (wt.%), Li et al. (2026) | Tensile creep rupture at 400 °C under 25–40 MPa; approximately 330 h life at 25 MPa | Direct stress-rupture result for an as-printed alloy strengthened by about 14 vol.% α-Al(FeMnNi)Si intermetallic nanophases; the longest separate thermal exposure reported was 168 h, not ≥1000 h | Creep and stress rupture ≥250 °C; no ≥1000 h exposure (li2026strongyetductile pages 6-11, li2026strongyetductile pages 11-16) |


*Table: Primary studies documenting actual creep or rupture testing at ≥250 °C, or unstressed thermal exposure lasting ≥1000 h at ≥250 °C. Creep duration and long-term aging are kept distinct to avoid treating censored or shorter creep tests as 1000-hour demonstrations.*

The clearest **stress-rupture measurements** include LPBF Al–10Ce: in Stinehart’s 2023 study, tensile specimens ruptured at 325 °C/21 MPa after 92.17 h, at 350 °C/21 MPa after 18.17 h, and at 350 °C/29 MPa after 6.1 h. Specimens tested at 300 °C/21 MPa and 300 °C/29 MPa were stopped *without rupture* after more than 765 and 546 h, respectively. The same work also measured compressive creep over 275–400 °C. The distinction matters: a 1000 h aging result does not demonstrate 1000 h creep life. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000061)

(2023) | Tensile creep/stress rupture at 300–350 °C: 300 °C/21 MPa ran **>765 h without rupture**; 325 °C/21 MPa ruptured at 92.17 h; 350 °C/21 MPa at 18.17 h; 350 °C/29 MPa at 6.1 h | Direct rupture-life measurements; the >765 h result is right-censored and **not** evidence of a ≥1000 h creep test | Creep and stress rupture ≥250 °C (pqac-00000061) |

(2020) | Compressive creep at 260 °C for 8 and 168 h | Approximate threshold stress was 40 MPa as fabricated versus 14 MPa after prior aging in the 8 h test; behavior converged after 168 h because grain-boundary Al₃Zr coarsened during testing | Creep ≥250 °C; no ≥1000 h exposure reported (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000033) |

(2023) | Tensile creep at 300 °C in as-fabricated and heat-treated conditions | Stress producing a minimum creep rate of 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹ fell from 56 MPa as fabricated to 30 MPa after 400 °C/200 h aging; heat treatment promoted precipitate-free zones and grain-boundary sliding | Creep ≥250 °C; aging was only 200 h (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000060) |

contexts.context: The excerpt provides creep data at 300 °C for AlSi10Mg alloys containing both Zr and Sc, rather than a clearly separated Sc-free, Zr-only alloy. Specimens were peak-aged for 96 h at 300 °C before compression creep testing. Creep behavior showed diffusional creep below approximately 20 MPa, with stress exponent n≈1, and dislocation creep at higher stresses, where apparent stress exponents were na=8–18. The pre-alloyed Zr-Sc alloy exhibited substantially better creep resistance than unmodified and master-alloyed material: at a strain rate of 10^-6 s^-1, the required stress was increased by a factor of 2.6, attributed to greater incorporation of Zr and Sc and more second-phase particles obstructing dislocations. The excerpt does not provide a complete table of applied stresses, individual creep rates, or rupture results; unmodified-alloy tests accumulated 94–522 h. For thermal aging at 300 °C, L12 Al3(Sc,Zr) precipitates formed while eutectic Si coarsened. Hardness plateaus were reported from 1–200 h, but no hardness value or mechanical result after ≥1000 h is given. The 1000 h reference concerns estimated Si diffusion distances (43 μm), not a reported 1000 h aging experiment.

For the Al–15Fe comparison, the as-built structure contains stable θ-Al13Fe4 around melt-pool boundaries and metastable spherical Al6Fe particles within a nanoscale α-Al/Al6Fe cellular structure. After 1000 h at 300 °C, the θ-phase morphology remained nearly unchanged, while the cellular structure dissolved into the α-Al matrix. Spherical Al6Fe particles grew and newly nucleated, and θ phase precipitated. Thermal exposure also produced numerous equiaxed grains and a more homogeneous microstructure. contexts.context: This excerpt reports primary tensile-creep measurements for laser-powder-bed-fused, scandium-free Al-10Ce, rather than the specific Al-11Ce-3Ni-1Mn, Al-Ce-Ni-Mn-Zr, Al-Ni-Fe-Zr, Al-Ce-Fe, or Al-7Ce-8Mg compositions listed in the question. Tests were conducted at 300–350°C and 21 or 29 MPa. At 300°C, testing was interrupted because of the long duration: 21 MPa produced 1.7% strain after more than 765 h, and 29 MPa produced 1.3% strain after more than 546 h. At 325°C and 21 MPa, rupture occurred after 92.17 h at 1.6% strain. At 350°C, 21 MPa caused rupture after 18.17 h at 3.7% strain, while 29 MPa caused rupture after 6.1 h; strain was unavailable because the specimen broke outside the marked gauge length. No strain-rate values or 1000-hour tests are reported in this excerpt. The fracture surfaces were predominantly flat and intergranular/brittle, with limited ductile dimpling. Microstructural observations showed LPBF-refined eutectic features, fading melt-pool boundaries with increasing temperature, grain-boundary denuded zones, and dislocation pile-up. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone measured creep, stress-rupture or long-exposure (1000 h or more) thermal stability at 250 C or above for a laser powder bed fusion aluminum alloy that contains no scandium, such as Al-Ce, Al-Fe-Zr, Al-Ni-Zr, Al-Mn-Zr or Al-Cu-Mn-Zr alloys?

Yes. **Yes.** Published studies report both creep or stress-rupture tests at ≥250 °C and *separate, unstressed* thermal exposures lasting ≥1000 h for scandium-free, laser-powder-bed-fused (LPBF) aluminum alloys. The distinction matters: a 1000 h aging result does not demonstrate 1000 h creep life. (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 1-2, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 7-9, sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 5-8, stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 39-47)

| Alloy / primary report | Eligible exposure or test | Verified finding | Category |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary Al–10Ce (wt.%), Stinehart et al. (2023) | Tensile creep/stress rupture at 300–350 °C: 300 °C/21 MPa ran **>765 h without rupture**; 325 °C/21 MPa ruptured at 92.17 h; 350 °C/21 MPa at 18.17 h; 350 °C/29 MPa at 6.1 h | Direct rupture-life measurements; the >765 h result is right-censored and **not** evidence of a ≥1000 h creep test | Creep and stress rupture ≥250 °C (stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 39-47) |
| Al–3.6Mg–1.2Zr and Al–2.9Mg–2.1Zr (wt.%), Griffiths et al. (2020) | Compressive creep at 260 °C for 8 and 168 h | Approximate threshold stress was 40 MPa as fabricated versus 14 MPa after prior aging in the 8 h test; behavior converged after 168 h because grain-boundary Al₃Zr coarsened during testing | Creep ≥250 °C; no ≥1000 h exposure reported (griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 1-2) |
| Al–8.6Cu–0.5Mn–0.9Zr (wt.%), Michi et al. (2023) | Tensile creep at 300 °C in as-fabricated and heat-treated conditions | Stress producing a minimum creep rate of 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹ fell from 56 MPa as fabricated to 30 MPa after 400 °C/200 h aging; heat treatment promoted precipitate-free zones and grain-boundary sliding | Creep ≥250 °C; aging was only 200 h (michi2023loadshufflingduring pages 30-33, michi2023loadshufflingduring pages 27-30) |
| Al–0.4Zr–1X (at.%), X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo or W, Ekaputra et al. (2026) | Compressive creep at 400 °C; separate **unstressed** aging at 400 °C for as long as 2016 h | Every ternary alloy was substantially more creep resistant than binary Al–0.4Zr. Mn and Cr precipitated during aging, whereas V, Mo and W remained almost entirely in solution after 2016 h; their room-temperature strengthening contribution remained broadly stable | Creep ≥250 °C **and** unstressed aging ≥1000 h (ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 1-4, ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 21-25) |
| Al–10Ce–8Mn (wt.%), Sisco et al. (2023) | **Unstressed** LPBF specimens aged at 400 °C for 1000 h | Metastable Al₂₀Mn₂Ce decomposed; Al₆Mn, Al₁₂Mn and Al₅₁Mn₇Ce₄ formed, while equilibrium Al₁₁Ce₃ remained. This report did not measure creep | Unstressed thermal stability ≥1000 h only (sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 5-8, sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 13-18) |
| Al–5.0Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr (wt.%, Alloy C), Mehta et al. (2023–2024) | **Unstressed** aging at 350 °C for 1000 h; separate detailed characterization after 24 h peak aging plus 1054 h, or 1078 h total | Hardness began declining after about 200 h and lost only 17–18 HV (about 13%) by 1000 h. At 1078 h total, precipitates occupied about 18 area% and included Cr-bearing Al₁₂Mn and Al₆Mn | Unstressed thermal stability ≥1000 h; no creep reported (mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 7-9, mehta2024roleofcr pages 3-4) |
| Al–15Fe (wt.%), Wang et al. (2022) | **Unstressed** exposure at 300 °C for 1000 h | Hardness decreased moderately from approximately 200 HV. The nanoscale α-Al/Al₆Fe cellular structure largely dissolved, spherical metastable Al₆Fe particles grew, and stable plate-shaped θ-Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitated | Unstressed thermal stability ≥1000 h only (wang2022microstructuralvariationsin pages 5-8, wang2022microstructuralvariationsin media a4102c0d) |
| Al–7.44Si–2.34Fe–1.79Mn–1.12Ni (wt.%), Li et al. (2026) | Tensile creep rupture at 400 °C under 25–40 MPa; approximately 330 h life at 25 MPa | Direct stress-rupture result for an as-printed alloy strengthened by about 14 vol.% α-Al(FeMnNi)Si intermetallic nanophases; the longest separate thermal exposure reported was 168 h, not ≥1000 h | Creep and stress rupture ≥250 °C; no ≥1000 h exposure (li2026strongyetductile pages 6-11, li2026strongyetductile pages 11-16) |


*Table: Primary studies documenting actual creep or rupture testing at ≥250 °C, or unstressed thermal exposure lasting ≥1000 h at ≥250 °C. Creep duration and long-term aging are kept distinct to avoid treating censored or shorter creep tests as 1000-hour demonstrations.*

The clearest **stress-rupture measurements** include LPBF Al–10Ce: in Stinehart’s 2023 study, tensile specimens ruptured at 325 °C/21 MPa after 92.17 h, at 350 °C/21 MPa after 18.17 h, and at 350 °C/29 MPa after 6.1 h. Specimens tested at 300 °C/21 MPa and 300 °C/29 MPa were stopped *without rupture* after more than 765 and 546 h, respectively. The same work also measured compressive creep over 275–400 °C. A different, Sc-free LPBF Al–7.44Si–2.34Fe–1.79Mn–1.12Ni alloy was reported to last approximately 330 h in tensile creep at 400 °C/25 MPa. None of these results establishes a ≥1000 h rupture life. (stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 31-39, stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 23-31, stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 39-47, li2026strongyetductile pages 6-11, li2026strongyetductile pages 11-16)

For the alloy families named in the question, **Al–Cu–Mn–Zr has direct creep data**: Michi and colleagues tested LPBF Al–8.6Cu–0.5Mn–0.9Zr at 300 °C. The stress associated with a minimum creep rate of 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹ was 56 MPa as fabricated, versus 30 MPa after a 400 °C/200 h pretreatment; this is evidence of creep measurement, not of 1000 h thermal stability. Griffiths and colleagues measured compressive creep of two Sc-free LPBF Al–Mg–Zr alloys at 260 °C, including an approximately 168 h test. Ekaputra and colleagues measured compressive creep of LPBF Al–0.4Zr–1X (at.%; X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo or W) at 400 °C; all five ternary compositions outperformed their binary Al–Zr comparator. (michi2023loadshufflingduring pages 30-33, michi2023loadshufflingduring pages 27-30, griffiths2020coarseningandcreep pages 1-2, ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 1-4, ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 21-25)

The **≥1000 h thermal-stability evidence** is also direct, but its conclusions differ by alloy. LPBF Al–10Ce–8Mn underwent 400 °C/1000 h exposure: the investigators observed decomposition of Al₂₀Mn₂Ce and formation of Al₆Mn, Al₁₂Mn and Al₅₁Mn₇Ce₄; this is measured phase evolution, *not* proof that the initial microstructure remained unchanged. For LPBF Al–5Mn–0.8Cr–0.6Zr (‘alloy C’), hardness fell by approximately 17–18 HV, or 13%, over 350 °C/1000 h; a related study characterized precipitates after 1078 h total at 350 °C. The suggestion that a different, Mg-containing variant would retain 140–150 HV after 1000 h was an **estimate**, not that variant’s measured result. (sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 5-8, sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 13-18, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 7-9, mehta2024roleofcr pages 3-4)

Two further long exposures broaden the evidence. LPBF Al–15Fe was examined after 300 °C/1000 h: hardness decreased moderately, the initial nanoscale Al/Al₆Fe cellular structure changed, and stable Al₁₃Fe₄ precipitated; the study’s hardness-versus-time figure includes the 1000 h measurement. In LPBF Al–0.4Zr–1X, exposure extended to **2016 h at 400 °C**: Mn and Cr showed precipitation, whereas V, Mo and W remained almost entirely in solution; the authors reported broadly stable room-temperature strengthening contributions from the ternary solutes. These are observations of *unstressed* specimens and should not be reported as creep lives. (wang2022microstructuralvariationsin pages 5-8, wang2022microstructuralvariationsin media a4102c0d, ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 1-4, ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 21-25)

**Bottom line:** the answer is unambiguously yes, including for Al–Ce, Al–Mn–Cr–Zr, Al–Cu–Mn–Zr and Al–Zr–Mn systems. What is substantially less established by the verified examples is **stress-rupture survival for ≥1000 h** at these temperatures: the cited ≥1000 h results are thermal-aging or microstructural measurements, while the specific rupture tests above ended sooner or were stopped before rupture. (stinehart2023creepresistanceand pages 39-47, mehta2023advancingnovelalmncrzr pages 7-9, sisco2023heterogeneousphasetransformation pages 13-18, ekaputra2026coarseningandcreepbehavior pages 1-4)

(2020) | Compressive creep at 260 °C for 8 and 168 h | Approximate threshold stress was 40 MPa as fabricated versus 14 MPa after prior aging in the 8 h test; behavior converged after 168 h because grain-boundary Al₃Zr coarsened during testing | Creep ≥250 °C; no ≥1000 h exposure reported (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000033) |

(2023) | Tensile creep at 300 °C in as-fabricated and heat-treated conditions | Stress producing a minimum creep rate of 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹ fell from 56 MPa as fabricated to 30 MPa after 400 °C/200 h aging; heat treatment promoted precipitate-free zones and grain-boundary sliding | Creep ≥250 °C; aging was only 200 h (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000060) |
| Al–0.4Zr–1X (at.%), X = Mn, Cr, V, Mo or W, Ekaputra et al. (2026) | Compressive creep at 400 °C; separate **unstressed** aging at 400 °C for as long as 2016 h | Every ternary alloy was substantially more creep resistant than binary Al–0.4Zr. Mn and Cr precipitated during aging, whereas V, Mo and W remained almost entirely in solution after 2016 h; their room-temperature strengthening contribution remained broadly stable | Creep ≥250 °C **and** unstressed aging ≥1000 h (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000035) |

This report did not measure creep | Unstressed thermal stability ≥1000 h only (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000063) |

(2023–2024) | **Unstressed** aging at 350 °C for 1000 h; separate detailed characterization after 24 h peak aging plus 1054 h, or 1078 h total | Hardness began declining after about 200 h and lost only 17–18 HV (about 13%) by 1000 h. (2026) | Tensile creep rupture at 400 °C under 25–40 MPa; approximately 330 h life at 25 MPa | Direct stress-rupture result for an as-printed alloy strengthened by about 14 vol.% α-Al(FeMnNi)Si intermetallic nanophases; the longest separate thermal exposure reported was 168 h, not ≥1000 h | Creep and stress rupture ≥250 °C; no ≥1000 h exposure (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000059) |
